# Core Development Contract

A Core change must first identify which kind of external behavior it changes: application capability, Vendor operation, lifecycle, data semantics, thread context, ownership, or failure outcome. As long as it is observable by the upper layers or the porting layer, it is an architectural contract change, and the corresponding Application or Platform contract and subsystem documentation should be updated at the same time.

## Choosing the Extension Boundary

| Capability to be added | Boundary to extend | Responsibilities Core should not be forced to take on |
|---|---|---|
| New SoC, chip, touch/knob/screen implementation | Platform port implements the existing Device/port contract and registers before dependent services start | Do not scatter chip registers, Vendor SDK types, or board-level conditions into Service, Framework, or Application |
| New logical data service | Service owns semantics, state, demand arbitration, caching, and error mapping; when hardware is needed, go through the Device contract | Do not let Vendor maintain application permissions, caching, and application state |
| New Sensor type/data semantics | Update the public unit/type/validity conventions, the Sensor Service's caching and demand model, and hook up the target device implementation | Do not add private fields only in a single board or JS wrapper |
| New audio encoding format | Implement a Decoder and add it to Audio Service initialization registration; comply with the Player output contract | Do not add Codec-specific parsing branches in the playback scheduling layer or speaker driver |
| New watch face semantic value | Extend the current static Metric name/source mapping, then decide whether to expose it via SNI/controls | Do not turn raw sensor types directly into stable semantics that all applications can understand |
| New LVGL component or JS API | The component owns its internal objects; SNI describes the owner and invalidation points of handles, strings, buffers, and callbacks | Do not expose raw pointers, and do not bypass the Activity/View/SNI lifecycle |
| Cross-thread deferred operation | Use the Dispatcher or the task queue already defined by that Service, and define the lifetime for user data | Do not treat the synchronous Event Bus as a queue, and do not enter JS/LVGL directly from an ISR |
| Notification delivery and persistence | First define the service, identity, permissions, queue/persistence, and backend delivery contract, then connect the UI | Do not mistake the message list overlay or the notification permission enumeration for the notification system |

Sensor, device type, and Metric currently do not define a general dynamic Provider selection or priority contract. Audio Decoder provides a registration extension boundary, but there is no secure hot-plug management yet. Each module should manage its lifecycle according to its actual extension contract, and they do not share one undefined Provider lifecycle.

## Dependencies and Ownership

- Framework/applications depend on the Service's semantic interface; Service depends on the Device type interface; Platform implements the Device/port contract. Dependencies cannot cross in reverse: Vendor does not depend on Activity, LVGL, SNI, or application objects.
- Sensor Service owns the per-type FIFO/latest cache, demand, and Native subscriber nodes; each subscriber releases only its own demand.
- Services such as Battery, Metric, and Config own their respective state snapshots; callers receive values/borrowed data or an agreed handle, and do not automatically gain ownership of the service's internal objects by reading.
- SPM owns the script program/Realm/context; Activity Controller owns the page stack and View; an LVGL parent object owns its subtree. View destroy, program stop, and engine generation changes are different invalidation points.
- The EPKG context owns package file handles and parse tables; preview values, manifest temporary results, and unpack targets are released by their respective agreed consumers. After the package context is closed, its borrowed pointers become invalid, and the installation flow will not continue to reference these pointers after closure.

An asynchronous callback needs at least an owner, a cancellation/destruction path, and a determinable generation or object liveness check. If a callback may arrive after the owner is paused/destroyed, the Realm is reset, or the target object is deleted, it must be discarded before entering the upper layers, and cannot be remedied by dangling pointer checks.

## Synchronous Broadcast and Deferred Work Are Not the Same Thing

| Mechanism | What guarantee the caller gets | Applicable boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Service function/Device op | Return value or immediate state within the current call stack; may synchronously trigger lower-layer operations | Parameters and values are handled per the function contract; a synchronous call returning only means that call completed, and the semantics of background work completion are defined by the specific service |
| Event Bus | Synchronously traverses subscribers on publish;`param`borrows the publisher's storage | State change broadcast; callbacks are short, and subscribers copy data that needs to be retained across callbacks |
| Dispatcher | After successful enqueue, executed in order by the Core main loop | Hand off from ISR/platform threads to a GUI/script-safe context; submission does not mean reliable persistence, and queue expansion failure may drop tasks; callback user data must survive until execution |
| SNI callback | Called into JS in the owner program's Realm after runtime checks | Must be constrained by program state, context pause, engine generation, and bound resource lifecycle |
| Sensor data subscriber |`eos_sensor_notify`synchronously called after updating the cache | The execution context inherits from the publisher; publishing from an ISR is only applicable when it has been confirmed that the entire downstream path can run in interrupt context |

When execution is deferred, the producer copies or queues the minimum necessary data, and then the target context reads or consumes it; data used by an asynchronous callback remains valid during execution. Interfaces that allow a callback to re-enter the same service define cancellation, nested broadcast, and deletion semantics; interfaces without defined reentrancy semantics do not support reentrancy.

## State and Failure Propagation

Device capability, device state, service state, and sample validity each express different semantics and are not merged into a single Boolean:

- Not registered/not supported means a certain device capability does not exist.
- READY/BUSY/ERROR are device-layer states, not directly equal to the service upper layer's authorization or business state.
-`valid`/sample timestamp expresses whether data was obtained; a numeric zero can be a valid reading.
- Synchronous operation failure is returned through that boundary's result; asynchronous sources report upward through readable state, invalid samples, or clearly defined events.

The Device ops table is a type-specific contract; the required field checks also differ for different registrars. The Capability contract defines how absence of a capability is discovered, the call result, service degradation behavior, state changes, and retry semantics. An empty callback or a no-op success does not mean the capability is supported.

The current Power/Display path does not provide unified hardware confirmation: PM first updates software state and then calls the platform power op, and some display ops are void. Core page state or events can only represent software state changes and cannot be elevated to proof of physical device success. When adding flows that require reliable confirmation, a contract that can return/report completion status should be explicitly introduced, rather than continuing to rely on the existing fire-and-forget assumption.

## Lifecycle Boundaries Cannot Be Merged```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ACTIVE
    ACTIVE --> SUSPENDED: Recent Apps 保留
    SUSPENDED --> ACTIVE: 恢复同一 program instance
    ACTIVE --> STOPPING: 驱逐 / 卸载 / 根替换 / fatal reset
    SUSPENDED --> STOPPING: 驱逐 / 卸载 / fatal reset
    STOPPING --> TERMINATED
```The diagram above only describes the Script Program. Activity/View also has independent enter/pause/resume/destroy and transition exit policies; device registration is currently statically established during platform startup, and there is no system-wide unified deinit/unregister at the service level. When modifying one of these lifecycles, you must check whether the references, callbacks, snapshots, and buffers of other owners are still alive.

## Core Change Self-Check

- Who initiates the request, and who calls the implementation? Along which path is the response or sample returned?
- Among Pull, Push, Subscribe, Event, or Stream, which models actually exist?
- Which layer stores state; what the consumer sees is a cache, a borrowed value, or a transfer of ownership?
- Is the callback synchronous, Dispatcher-deferred, or timer-dispatched? Is the execution context safe?
- Are the stop and destroy of Service/Activity/Program/Device each explicit?
- How are missing capability, initialization failure, device offline, invalid sample, and cancellation each manifested?
- Should the new capability be connected through an existing extension point, or does it require changing the public contract? Which platform and application documents are updated accordingly?

For related role boundaries, see [Application Contract](./application_contract)and [Platform/Vendor Contract](./platform_contract).

# Application and Framework Contract

This page defines the system boundaries that application and Framework developers can rely on. Built-in C applications in the system work through Activities, services, and UI components; script applications use EPKG identity and can only access the Core through the`eos`/`lv`interfaces exposed by SNI. Neither can hold Vendor drivers or device operation tables. SPM only owns the program and Realm lifecycle of script Applications/Watchfaces, and is not the unified entry point for the lifecycle of all built-in C pages.

## Launch Identity and Running Instance

The`manifest.json`ID of an installation package is the application/watchface identity. Launch requests target this ID, not a file name or display name. The application manager is responsible for validating the installed identity and handing the request to SPM; SPM exclusively owns the Script Engine Core and Realm lifecycle. Only one unterminated script program can exist for an ID at a time: foreground switching typically resumes an existing instance and cannot start a second Realm.

Package installation starts from a single EPKG context: reading metadata can be used for preview; installation must also fully validate all entries, then unpack according to`package_type`and update the installation identity. A successful preview, completed transfer, or the existence of a package file does not equal successful installation; the caller should use the installation result and events to determine the final state.```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User as 系统入口 / 调用方
    participant Manager as 应用管理器
    participant Activity as Activity Controller
    participant SPM
    participant Engine as Script Engine
    participant Recent as Recent Apps

    User->>Manager: 请求打开已安装 ID
    Manager->>Activity: 创建/恢复 App Activity 与 View
    Activity-->>User: 新启动时先显示 loading 页面
    alt 新建程序
        Manager->>SPM: 同步运行已安装脚本
        SPM->>Engine: 创建 owner Realm 并执行 main.js
        Engine-->>SPM: 启动结果 / 异常
    else Recent Apps 恢复
        Manager->>SPM: 恢复同一 suspended instance
        SPM->>SPM: 恢复 context 资源，不重跑 main.js
    end
    SPM-->>Manager: 实例 ID 与程序状态
    Manager->>Activity: 绑定实例和 generation
    User->>Activity: 离开前台
    Activity->>Recent: 页面过渡后提交停放/销毁策略
    Recent->>SPM: 挂起或按实例停止
```When a brand-new application is launched, the Activity first establishes a loading page, then`spm_app_run`synchronously executes the script on the calling thread; during script initialization the main loop cannot process normal UI work, and the loading mask can only provide drawing feedback and cannot let JS run in parallel. Program resumption reuses the same instance and Realm saved by Recent Apps, does not re-execute`main.js`, and does not create duplicate parallel copies. Watchfaces use the root Activity replacement flow, with the watchface manager completing the program switch via SPM.

Page transitions and program lifecycle are two different things. An Activity can pause or destroy a page while retaining the program; when Recent Apps suspends, the program and some resources may still exist; only eviction, uninstallation, root watchface replacement, or a fatal engine reset enters a full stop. Applications must not directly call`script_engine`to start, resume, or clean up script programs.

## Capability Consumption Model

| Capability | Application-side interaction | Validity and end responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| Sensor (Native Core) | Pull FIFO/latest, or Push subscription callback; when there is a sampling demand, the service arbitrates. | latest returns invalid/not found when there is no sample; a zero value can still be valid. Callback parameters are only borrowed during the synchronous notification; Native subscriptions should be cancelled by the registering owner when no longer in use. |
| Sensor (JS) | There is currently no raw Sensor subscription interface; you can read the`eos.sensor`cache, or use`eos.metric`semantic values. | Metric samples carry`valid`/`stale`; subscriptions are bound to the program SNI context, and it is not guaranteed that each callback triggers one hardware sample.`eos.sensor.setSamplePeriod`uses a single compatibility demand per type, not a demand isolated per script/application; multiple callers will share and update it. |
| Battery | Native Pull current snapshot, or subscribe to change events; Metric provides semantic battery level values. | Invalid until a valid report is received; percentage/charging events are triggered by threshold changes, not broadcast on every hardware sample. |
| Metric | Pull once, or periodically notified by SNI timer. | SNI saves the owner program/generation; JS will not be called when the program is inactive, and unsubscribing or context cleanup releases the subscription. Destroying an Activity alone does not automatically mean the program is destroyed; data demands that are no longer needed should be actively cancelled by the application. |
| System events (Native Framework) | C modules can subscribe to state changes such as installation, power, and pages. |`eos_event_post`is a synchronous broadcast, and parameters are borrowed during the callback; to retain data after the callback returns, it must be copied. Unsubscribing is the responsibility of the subscribing module. Currently JS has no general Event Bus API and can only use the various registered dedicated callback interfaces. |
| Permission requests | JS requests are completed asynchronously by the authorization UI, and the result is returned via a script callback; Native services return the authorization status. | Requests may be denied, queued, or unable to call back due to an invalid program context; initiating a request itself does not mean authorization has completed. |
| Audio | Playback/recording requests synchronously return whether startup succeeded; PCM supply and hardware output then continue. | Speaker and microphone capabilities are independent; there is currently no general JS playback completion callback contract. Playback resources are held by the service, and the application stops or pauses through the service. |
| Time | Service synchronously Pulls the platform date and time. | Core has no clock update Push stream or unified time-sync completion event; the timezone/time-sync source belongs to the platform. |
| Display / Power | Framework requests brightness, sleep, AOD, or wakeup; power state changes are observed via synchronous system events. | Software state does not equal physical hardware confirmation; some operations are void/fire-and-forget, and specific platform capabilities may be missing. |
| Haptics | Framework requests feedback intents such as tick/buzz/long-vibration. | Device operations have no return value, and there is currently no per-vibration completion/failure event; the application cannot confirm that physical feedback has occurred. |
| Files and configuration | File/JSON operations are synchronous path operations;`eos.config`uses the current script ID to construct the application/watchface configuration file. | Handles become invalid after closing, and dynamic values are released according to the owning API. The general Storage API does not automatically isolate paths based on script identity, and a path prefix itself does not constitute a sandbox. |
| State / Log | State is synchronous reading and updating of persistent state; Log receives formatted messages via a listener. | The log listener executes synchronously and the message buffer is only valid within the callback; system state is not application configuration; logs have no background queue guarantee. |
| Notifications | There is currently no general application notification delivery API, notification broker, or persistent queue. | The`notification`permission category and message list UI do not mean that applications can publish/read system notifications. |

Metric currently has one visible validity exception:`battery.charging`folds the Battery Service's invalid/uninitialized state into`false`and still marks it as valid. If JS needs to determine whether a battery reading exists, it should also check`battery.percent.valid`; Native can use the Battery State validity query. This behavior is a current implementation limitation, not a general rule for all boolean Metrics.

Native Sensor's Push callback executes synchronously in the context that calls`eos_sensor_notify`; if the Vendor enters notification from an ISR, all consumers will also execute in that context. Therefore the platform should publish in a task/main loop context where Core callbacks can be safely executed; interrupts should only collect/queue unless the entire downstream path is explicitly safe to run in an ISR. JS metric callbacks are dispatched by the LVGL timer in the Core main loop and enter the owning Realm.

## Cleanup of Pages, Programs, and Callbacks

- An Activity owns the page View; deleting the View invalidates its LVGL child objects, tree-node handles, and page callbacks. Old View pointers must not be saved and used across destroy or root replacement.
- SPM owns the script program, Realm, and program-level SNI context. Stopping/resetting invalidates all JS handles and callbacks of the old generation; SNI re-validates the owner, state, and generation when the callback enters.
- Activity pause and SPM suspend are not equivalent. While the program is retained by Recent Apps, script-subscribed objects may still be alive; when hardware/service demands need to be stopped, they should be explicitly cancelled or released in the lifecycle callback.
- Native callback`user_data`, event`param`, and synchronously passed data pointers are managed by the subscriber according to the contract; the system will not automatically discover and unregister arbitrary C pointers merely because an Activity is destroyed.
- Timeout, no device, unauthorized, no sample, and script exception are different results. Applications should branch on result/status/validity fields, and must not infer success from zero, an empty object, or a callback that did not occur.

## Boundaries Application Development Should Not Bypass

- Use the Activity Controller to manage pages; do not directly modify the Activity stack, delete system-managed Views, or reattach parked pages.
- Use services or registered SNI interfaces to access sensors, audio, storage, power, and display; do not rely on device lookup order or Vendor implementation details.
- New JS APIs can only be exposed through SNI descriptions and owner-bound callback/resource paths; do not expose raw native pointers.
- EPKG preview is only suitable for displaying metadata and cannot replace full validation and installation results.

For details, see [Activity](./framework/activity), [Application Management](./framework/app), [Recent Apps](./framework/app/recent_apps), [Script Runtime and SNI](./runtime), and the corresponding service pages.

# Platform Port and Driver

Platform Port is the integration layer that consumes ElenixOS Core; it implements the port/device contract declared by Core and connects BSP, Vendor SDK, interrupts, DMA, clocks, file system, and GUI/HAL to the OS. The port header files in the Core repository describe the interfaces; chip-specific implementations belong to the actual platform engineering.

## What the platform provides to Core

The integration project first prepares the execution environment required by the OS (clocks, critical sections/scheduling, memory, file system, and LVGL display/input), then registers the device operations that the target actually has, and initializes services before the relevant services are enabled. Core does not guess on behalf of the platform which Vendor drivers exist, nor does it have a unified discovery, hot-plug, or shutdown scheduler covering all devices.

There are two categories of operation direction:

- Core/Service synchronously calls Device ops to request actions such as enable, sample rate, display/power settings, audio open/submit, etc. Platform operations should be bounded and return quickly; if the work is slow, queue it to a platform task and then report the result through that device contract.
- The platform pushes samples/status to Core, or pulls real-time values when Core calls. Vendors need to convert hardware units and board-level coordinates into OS common data semantics before reporting, and propagate invalid/error states as specified.

## Responsibilities drivers must not have

- Do not decide cross-consumer sample rates, volume/power business policies, or application permissions on behalf of the Service.
- Do not directly execute application/JS callbacks, do not create or destroy Activity/View, and do not touch LVGL/JerryScript.
- Do not assume that another platform implementation has the same capabilities as this board; missing optional operations must be identifiable, and call failures must be returned/reported according to the device contract.
- Do not retain borrowed buffers beyond the owner's lifecycle; asynchronous DMA/tasks must stop and confirm no further access before Core reclaims memory or shuts down the device.

## Interrupts, tasks, and callbacks

Vendor callbacks do not automatically switch to a unified thread. Device ops are usually executed in the synchronous call context of the initiating service; Event Bus callbacks execute synchronously in the publisher's context; the Dispatcher queues short tasks to the Core main loop. Sensor reports enter Native consumers synchronously on the call stack of`eos_sensor_notify`; battery report changes also publish events synchronously. Therefore, the ISR can handle acquisition or queuing; if the downstream chain is not confirmed as a whole to be ISR-safe, the platform needs to defer first, then call the entry point that dispatches consumers.

Various operations have different execution contexts: Time's pull, Platform control operations, Battery acquisition, and Sensor sample publishing each follow their own conventions.`callback`in function names does not mean the operation is necessarily asynchronous or thread-safe; platform ports handle context and buffer requirements according to the corresponding documentation.

## Data/error propagation```mermaid
flowchart LR
    HW[SoC / Sensor / Codec / Display] -->|原始值、状态| Adapt[Vendor Driver / Adapter]
    Adapt -->|规范化后的契约数据| Device[Device / Port API]
    Device --> Service[Core Service]
    Service -->|值、有效性、错误、事件| App[Framework / Application]
    Service -->|同步操作请求| Device
```Synchronous operation errors are returned along the call result; asynchronous devices update status or submit data in the reporting path. A sample value of zero is not a fault flag; it is necessary to distinguish between no sample yet, stale sample, device error, and a legitimate zero value. The fact that a feature is available in a software simulator does not mean the target hardware has implemented it.

Sensor coordinate/time/sampling requirements, Audio buffering, Display/Power states, and device registration order are defined by [platform port contract](./platform_contract); the Device operation table and capability lifecycle are described in [device contract](./device_architecture_design).

--- title: System Architecture --- # System Architecture ElenixOS consists of a portable Core and platform integration. Core defines the application model, program and page management, system services, device contracts, and foundational runtime interfaces; platform integration connects these interfaces to a specific SoC, BSP, Vendor HAL, and hardware. Applications depend on the public models and capabilities provided by Core, not on a particular chip or driver. Platform differences are confined to interface implementations and device capabilities, which are conveyed to Core through the corresponding contracts. Script Applications and Watch Faces use installation packages as their deployment unit. The EPKG format contract defines installation identity, the packaging of program and resource files, and verification boundaries; the Installer / Loader verifies and unpacks according to the contract, and the runtime consumes the installed application identity and files. EPKG is a Package Contract shared by development tools and the system installer, and is not a private format of the runtime or Platform. For the format definition, see [EPKG v1 Package Format](./package_format); for the application runtime model, see [Application Management Module](./framework/app). When understanding ElenixOS, it should be viewed as multiple cooperating architectural domains managed by different owners, rather than a single "application calls driver" layer chain. The diagram below shows the main relationships: Program/Runtime, Activity/UI, and system services are different parts of Core; dashed lines indicate that the platform implements interfaces defined by Core; data and state can return in the opposite direction of control requests. ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph APP["Applications and Installation Identity"] NativeApp["Built-in Native Application"] JSApp["JavaScript Application"] Package["EPKG Package

Core and applications do not depend on Vendor types or register interfaces. - **Isolation of applications from hardware.** Applications use system capabilities through the Framework and public Service APIs. Script applications can only access registered Native APIs through SNI. Applications do not directly call device operation tables or drivers. - **Separation of policy and mechanism.** Services hold system state, shared policy, and cross-consumer coordination; device contracts define the operation and data semantics between Core and platform implementations; the platform is responsible for actual hardware operations and platform backends. - **Objects managed by owner.** Programs, Activities/Views, Service state, and platform-registered devices each have their own lifecycle owner. An object being referenced or associated by another layer does not imply a transfer of ownership. - **Capabilities expressed by contract.** Platform capabilities are not assumed to be identical everywhere. The expression of missing capabilities, failed operations, or invalid data is defined by the corresponding device type and Service contract; upper layers handle them according to public results. - **Upper layers depend on stable boundaries.** Applications, Service extensions, and platform ports enter the system through Framework/Service APIs, Core extension points, and Device/port contracts respectively, without propagating platform differences into the application model. ## Architectural Domains | Architectural Domain | Problems Solved and Main Objects | What It Is Not Responsible For | |---|---|---| | Application and Installation Identity | Represents the stable identity, manifest, and files of a built-in Native application or an installed script application. EPKG is the delivery/installation unit; after the Installer verifies and unpacks, the Application Framework manages the installed identity and resources. | Not equivalent to a runtime instance, an Activity, or a View tree. For in-package region definitions, see [EPKG v1 Package Format](./package_format). | | Program and JavaScript Runtime | Creates and manages Program Instances, Realms, and SNI contexts for script applications, and executes JavaScript. SPM manages program lifecycle, Script Engine executes scripts, and SNI provides the controlled JS/Native boundary. | Does not manage the global Activity page stack, nor replace Service system policy. Built-in Native applications typically have no SPM Program. | | Activity and UI | Represents the system root page, navigation pages, and their entry, pause, resume, and destruction; the Activity Controller manages page relationships, an Activity owns its View, and the View is rooted in the LVGL object tree. | Does not own the JavaScript Realm; an Activity is not an alias for a Program. | | Application Framework | Provides high-level application-facing models and coordinates application/watchface identity, launch entry points, page navigation, and public system capabilities. It delegates Program management to SPM and page relationships to the Activity Controller. | Does not directly implement chip drivers, nor take over the lifecycle of Services or page objects. | | System Services | Provides shared capabilities to the system and applications, and holds state, caches, policy, demand arbitration, or scheduling when needed. Native Framework can use public Service APIs, and script applications use the corresponding registered APIs through SNI. | Does not provide the hardware implementation of a particular board; Service policy should not be moved into Vendor drivers. | | Device Abstraction and Port Interfaces | Device Contracts define the operations, state, and data boundaries between Core and device implementations by device type; port contracts provide platform foundational interfaces such as file system, memory, and critical sections. | Does not define application semantics, nor imply that all devices share a single registration, hot-plug, or shutdown flow. | | Platform Integration | Combines platform startup, port implementations, device registration, device adapters, and BSP/Vendor backends to connect Core contracts to the target hardware. | Does not decide application permissions, page transitions, Program state, or Service policy. | | Core Infrastructure | Provides common support such as initialization, main loop, memory, events, and scheduling for Core subsystems. | Does not replace application/page/device owners, nor constitute a unified queue applicable to all asynchronous behavior. | The Core boundary in the diagram is composed of Framework/UI, Program Runtime, Services, Device Abstraction, port contracts, and infrastructure. Device and port interfaces belong to Core's abstraction surface; the concrete implementations of the interfaces reside in Platform Integration. Whether a given device operation is optional, how its absence is discovered, and how state is reported all depend on that type's own contract and cannot be derived from a generic registration diagram. ## Application, Program, Activity, and View These concepts describe different stages and different objects: | Concept | Meaning | Primary Owner | |---|---|---| | Package | An EPKG installation container containing installation identity metadata, entry scripts, and bundled files. Installation verifies and expands its contents. | Package / Installer | | Installed Application | The application identity and files that have been installed and can be discovered, ordered, and launched by a stable ID. Built-in Native Applications may not be installed as script packages. | Application Framework | | Program Instance | An executable instance of a script application or watchface, associated with a stable application ID, instance ID, Realm, and SNI context. A second unterminated script instance is not created in parallel for the same ID. | SPM | | Activity | A system or application page and its state in the root page/page stack. An Activity typically owns one page View. | Activity Controller and the owning page flow | | View | The LVGL page root object of an Activity and its UI subtree. Deleting a parent object can invalidate child objects and reference handles. | Activity / LVGL object tree | | JS Realm | The isolated context in which a Program executes JavaScript. SNI installs supported Native bindings in this Realm. | Program / SPM in cooperation with Script Engine | The Program of a script application can be associated with an application Activity and its child pages; when a Program goes through multiple page states, it does not thereby become multiple Programs. Conversely, a system page or built-in Native Activity can exist without a script Program. Application identity is stable across multiple launches, while a Program Instance represents one of those execution lifetimes that has not yet terminated. Switching the foreground page first changes the Activity/UI state; upper-layer flows such as Recent Apps then decide whether the program and pages are temporarily parked for restoration or fully evicted. Restoration reattaches the original instance and page state, rather than rebuilding the Activity as a Realm. On destruction, the Activity Controller cleans up page objects, SPM cleans up Program/Realm/SNI resources, and associated resources are finalized according to each owner's contract. ## Runtime and Native System Boundary The JavaScript Runtime resides in Core's script execution domain. Application code is executed by the Script Engine in the Realm owned by the Program; SPM creates, restores, suspends, and stops Programs, and coordinates the runtime resources associated with that instance. SNI is the boundary between the Realm and the Native System: it only installs registered `eos`, `lv`, and other bindings into the script, and brings parameters, return values, handles, and callbacks into the Native implementation according to the binding contract. Therefore, a JS application cannot directly call a Native C function just because it exists; only capabilities that are explicitly registered and become script APIs are visible to JS. Native resources are still managed by their Native owner, and a JS reference itself does not transfer ownership of Activity, View, Service, or device objects. When page objects and script programs end, they are invalidated and cleaned up along the owner paths of pages and SNI/Program respectively. ## Framework, Service, Device, and Platform These four exist separately because they answer different questions: | Part | Question Answered | Architectural Responsibility | |---|---|---| | Framework | What system model do applications work with? | Provides the application/watchface model and high-level coordination entry points; coordinates page and program owners without holding ownership on their behalf. | | Service | Which system component holds shared policy and state? | Implements device-independent service semantics, caching, request coordination, and system/application-facing results. The state actually held by different Services is not entirely the same. | | Device Abstraction / Contract | How does Core describe a given type of device capability? | Defines typed boundaries, device state, and corresponding operation/data semantics for Services and platform implementations. Different types may adopt different patterns. | | Platform / Vendor | How are these operations implemented on the target chip? | Implements port/device interfaces, integrates with BSP, HAL, drivers, and concrete resources, and returns data or state according to device contracts. | Typical capability control is initiated by an Application, enters a Service through the Framework or a public Service API, and then reaches the Platform implementation through a Device Contract; data and state are obtained by the platform and returned to upper layers through the corresponding Device/Service. The Framework's high-level model does not replace Service policy, Services do not need to know Vendor chip details, and Vendors do not own application-level policy. ## Three Mutually Independent Lifecycles ElenixOS does not merge programs, pages, and devices into a single "application object". Independence means that state and lifecycle owners are different; it does not mean that any combination of states is valid; the Framework, Recent Apps, and each owner are responsible for coordination during cross-domain operations. | Lifecycle | Owner and Managed Objects | Relationship with Other Lifecycles | |---|---|---| | Program lifecycle | SPM manages script Programs, Realms, and SNI contexts, and performs start, resume, suspend, and stop. | Page transitions can occur while a Program is still retained; suspending a Program is not equivalent to destroying the Activity/View. | | Activity / UI lifecycle | The Activity Controller manages the root Activity, page stack, and page transitions; Activities/Views are paused, resumed, parked, or destroyed according to page rules. | An Activity can belong to a script application or be a Native/system page without a Program; page destruction also need not be equivalent to immediate Realm destruction. | | Device / Service lifecycle | Platform Integration establishes target platform devices and port implementations; Core Services hold their own state, caches, and consumer demands. | These system-level objects do not follow the launch or exit of a single application; cleanup of application requests or subscriptions is managed separately by the corresponding Service contract. | This separation allows the system to save resumable script execution state, handle page transitions independently, and continue providing shared device capabilities during application switching. Parking, eviction, and error recovery involving multiple types of objects must be coordinated by the corresponding owners, and the caller cannot arbitrarily choose a destruction order. ## Dependencies, Control, Data, and Ownership A single function call only indicates a local control relationship and cannot by itself indicate system dependencies, data returns, or resource ownership: | Relationship | Approximate Direction | Description | |---|---|---| | Architectural dependency | Applications call Services through the Framework / public Service APIs; Services use Core contracts to access devices. | Platform Integration implements interfaces defined by Core; upper layers do not depend on a specific Vendor. JS applications use public bindings through SNI. | | Control request | An Application initiates a request, the Framework / Service executes policy and calls the Device, and the Platform implements the device operation. | The Service decides how to use the device according to its own policy; the direction of the request does not change the owner of the interface. | | Data and state | The platform implementation provides data, which is processed by the Device / Service and then handed to the Framework / Application. | Data is validated, normalized, cached, or arbitrated according to the specific contract; models such as Push, Pull, and callback are specified by the corresponding subsystem. | | Lifecycle and ownership | The owner of each object manages it separately | SPM manages script programs, the Activity Controller manages pages, Services manage their own state, and platform integration manages platform implementations and registration. Mutual references do not imply a transfer of ownership. | | Error propagation | From the boundary where the error occurs toward consumers | Synchronous results, state, invalid data, or asynchronous notifications vary by device/Service; ElenixOS does not assume that all hardware uses the same success confirmation mechanism. | ## System-Level Stable Boundaries - Applications depend on public Framework/Service capabilities, not on the SoC, Vendor HAL, drivers, or device operation tables. - JavaScript can only enter the Native System through bindings registered by SNI; Native functions do not automatically become JS APIs. - Programs, Activities/Views, Service state, and platform-registered devices are managed by different owners; cross-domain coordination cannot merge or bypass these owners. - Services hold system-level policy and state; Platform/Vendor implements device mechanisms and complies with type contracts, without taking over application semantics. - Platform capabilities and the manner of their absence are expressed by the corresponding Device/Service contracts; porting cannot assume that a capability present on one development board is common to all platforms. - Extensions must choose the boundary consistent with capability ownership: application entry points enter the Application Framework, system policy enters Services, hardware capabilities enter Device Contracts and platform implementations, and script APIs enter public SNI bindings. ## Continue Reading by Development Role - For package format, region semantics, verification, and signature reservation, see [EPKG v1 Package Format](./package_format); # Activity Pages

Activity is the sole abstraction for page lifecycle and page switching. It describes how pages relate within the root Activity, the normal page stack, and the parked application sub-stack; it is not a substitute for script programs.

## Activity Model

Current Activity types include normal application pages, input pages, application lists, the current watchface, watchface lists, lock screen, Recent Apps, and Native App Debugger. App Debugger is an independent tool page type, not an alias for the system App List.

The system has a separately managed root Activity, typically the current watchface. Normal Activities are pushed onto the page stack; on return, the Activity controller selects the previous page and handles the exit strategy of the current page. An Activity typically owns one View, which is its LVGL page root object.

## Root Page and Page Stack

The root Activity is not destroyed by normal `back` operations. Watchface switching uses the root replacement flow; the old root and its View/script resources are destroyed with the replacement, and the new root becomes the system's new bottom page. Applications and system pages can be pushed onto the normal stack; an application's sub-pages can also be parked and restored as a whole by Recent Apps.

Page return, opening new pages, and restoring Recent Apps must all be performed through the Activity controller. Callers must not directly alter the Activity stack chain or re-attach a parked View to an arbitrary parent object.

## Lifecycle and Exit Strategy

The Activity lifecycle includes enter, pause, resume, and destroy:

- On enter, the View and content used for the first time by the page are established.
- Pause means the page has left the foreground but may still be resumed; it is not equivalent to destruction.
- Resume means the same Activity becomes the active page again.
- After destruction, the View, page resources, and the Activity itself can no longer be used.

Activity lifecycle hooks correspond to these transitions:

| Hook | Current Trigger Semantics |
|---|---|
| `on_enter` | Called once when the Activity first enters the current page flow; the page View is typically established here. |
| `on_pause` | Called when the current Activity leaves the foreground; when the application sub-stack is suspended, called in order from the top of the stack to AppRoot. It does not itself determine whether the page is kept or destroyed; the exit strategy determines subsequent lifecycle. |
| `on_resume` | Called when an Activity that has already been entered returns to the foreground; when the application sub-stack is restored, called in order from AppRoot to the current page. |
| `on_destroy` | Called when the Activity terminates, before its View is deleted and the Activity storage is released. |

When returning from an Activity, a path that selects `DESTROY` destroys the current page without calling its `on_pause`; the page being returned to executes `on_resume` after the old page's destruction is finalized. These hooks describe the page lifecycle and do not change SPM's independent ownership of the associated script Program.

Page transitions explicitly select `KEEP`, `DESTROY`, or `SUSPEND`. Before the transition completes, the old page may still be referenced by animation snapshots or return animations; cleanup must be performed by the transition finalization path. A parked Activity must not use the normal direct destruction interface; eviction should be completed through the Recent Apps/per-instance cleanup flow.

## Pages, Scripts, and Object Ownership

An Activity owns its page View; deleting an LVGL parent object may cascade-delete child widgets. A script program owns Realm and SNI resources, but must not delete system-managed Views by bypassing the Activity lifecycle. After an Activity or View is destroyed, C pointers, script handles, and callbacks must all be considered invalid.

After a page switch completes, a system event is published synchronously. The View pointer in the event is valid only for the lifetime guaranteed by the publisher; subscribers do not thereby acquire ownership of that View.

## Architecture Constraints

- Activity lifecycle can only be driven by the Activity controller and its owning managers.
- Direct destruction applies only to Activities that are not on the stack, not visible, and not parked; the current page, root page, and recent application pages must use their dedicated flows.
- An Activity's View can only be set during the permitted enter flow; a running page must not arbitrarily replace or delete system-managed Views.
- Page transitions must not rely on destroy/suspend flags left by the caller; exit semantics must belong to the current transition.
- App Debugger must remain an independent Activity type and must not reuse the App List's animations and business routes.
- The root page should be accessed through root Activity semantics; the old watchface getter is retained only for compatibility and is not the recommended boundary for new code.

## Lifecycle Flow

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph AppStart["Application Startup"]
        AppManager["Application Manager"] --> SPMStart["SPM creates or restores Program"]
        SPMStart --> CreateActivity["Activity creates application page"]
        CreateActivity --> CreateView["Enter page and establish View"]
        CreateView --> UpdateUI["SNI / Application updates UI"]
    end

    subgraph AppBackground["Application Leaves Foreground"]
        ExitPolicy["Activity computes exit strategy"] --> Transition["Complete page transition and detach page stack"]
        Transition --> RecentApps["Recent Apps parks or evicts"]
        RecentApps --> SPMStop["SPM suspends or stops the corresponding Program"]
    end

    subgraph WatchfaceSwitch["Watchface Switch"]
        WatchfaceManager["Watchface Manager"] --> ValidatePackage["Validate target package"]
        ValidatePackage --> ReplaceRoot["Replace root Activity"]
        ReplaceRoot --> StopOld["Stop old watchface program and resources"]
        StopOld --> EnterNew["Enter new root page"]
    end
```

For the application perspective on startup, suspension, and asynchronous resource boundaries, see [Application Contract](../../application_contract); for owner rules across Activity/SPM/SNI, see [Core Development Contract](../../core_development_contract).

# Device Contract

The Device Layer is the typed boundary between Service/Core and the platform implementation. It provides a registerable implementation entry point, state, and operations specific to that device type; it does not own application semantics, sampling/power policies, page lifecycle, or JS callbacks.

## Two Directions

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Service[OS Service] -->|Synchronous control request| Device[Device Contract]
    Device -->|Call registered ops| Port[Platform Implementation]
    Port -->|Sample / State / Sync result| Device
    Device -->|Capabilities and results| Service
    Service -->|Read / Subscribe / Event| Consumer[Framework / Application]
```

Control and data flow in different directions. The Service requests operations, and the Device invokes the platform through the registered operation table; for data-type devices, the platform pushes data or provides pull values according to its own protocol; the Service is then responsible for caching, arbitration, normalization, validity, and consumer-facing notification. The device layer does not automatically convert hardware callbacks into main loop tasks, nor does it automatically retry.

## Registration and Availability

The target platform registers the implementation of that type before the dependent Service is initialized. Successful registration only means the operation entry point has been registered; it does not mean the device is currently available, that every optional capability exists, or that future operations will succeed. Device state is used to represent the ready/busy/error defined by that type's contract; operation return codes describe the result of a single request, and the two cannot substitute for each other.

Device types define their own operation tables, required items, optional items, and return semantics. Display, power, audio, vibration, time, battery, and sensors do not have a unified `init/read/notify/deinit` interface. Missing capabilities may only be represented by NULL when that type explicitly allows them to be optional; the Service/caller needs to check for unsupported or device-missing results.

Currently, Sensor Device supports registering multiple instances by name, but Sensor Service binds one default device for each Sensor Type at initialization; registration order determines the default instance, and the Service has no dynamic selection, priority, or failover. Most other Devices are singletons. This model is not a general-purpose multi-provider framework, and the platform cannot assume that devices can be replaced or unregistered online.

## Data, Memory, and Lifecycle

- The Device Operation table is provided by the platform implementation, and Core holds a reference to it; the implementation and operation table must remain alive for the duration of the registration's validity.
- Sensor data is reported by the platform to the Service; the Service copies samples and manages the FIFO/latest itself. Subscription callback pointers are borrowed until the end of the current synchronous callback.
- Battery raw measurements are reported by the platform, and the Service copies them into service state; change Events are dispatched synchronously, and `param` is passed only as borrowed state.
- The Microphone's shared DMA buffer is allocated by the Audio Service and passed to the device; Core may reclaim it only after the device has stopped. The ownership of the Speaker's borrow/enqueue buffer is currently not fully specified by the public operation table and should be treated as an unclosed contract.
- Core currently has no unified device hotplug, registration revocation, or shutdown/deinit flow for all devices. The requests, subscribers, and caches owned by each Service must be managed by the lifecycle of the Service to which they belong.

## Extension Rules

When adding new hardware to an existing Device Type, register it before the initialization of the Service that consumes it, and follow the unit, context, state, and buffer contracts. If new application semantics or state policies are needed, extend/add a Service rather than stuffing business rules into the Device operation table. If what is being added is an entirely new Sensor Type, the public data type, units, coordinate/time semantics, caching, and sampling requirement behavior must also be defined at the same time.

For specific Vendor startup order, data reporting, and ISR boundaries, see [Platform/Vendor Contract](./platform_contract); for how applications consume Services, see [Application Contract](./application_contract).

## Overview

ElenixOS adopts a layered architecture design with the core principle that **the upper layer sends control instructions, and the lower layer only reports status**. This design achieves separation of concerns, maintaining loose coupling between system layers while facilitating porting and extensibility.

```
driver → Status Report
        ↓
device manager updates state
        ↓
service queries state
```

## Architecture Layers

### Layer Hierarchy

```
Application Layer (Application)
    ↓ Control Instructions (OPS)
Service Layer (Service Layer)
    ↓ Query/Control
Device Manager (Device Manager)
    ↓ Status Report
Driver Layer (Driver)
```

### Design Constraints

**Service Layer**
- Provides standard API interfaces upward
- Can only use devices, cannot manage device information
- Obtains device instances through device manager and operates on device OPS
- Forbidden from directly calling driver layer code

**Device Framework**
- Unified device instance management through device manager
- All devices must provide `register` function for registration
- Device state can only be reported from driver to device manager
- Service layer can only obtain device state by querying state machine status

**Driver Layer**
- Implemented by the porter
- Ensures upper layer can operate lower-level hardware through implementing OPS
- Responsible for hardware status collection and reporting

## Service Layer

### Service List

| Service Name | Service File | Description |
|-------------|--------------|-------------|
| Sensor Service | `eos_service_sensor.c/.h` | Sensor sampling and data processing |
| Display Service | `eos_service_display.c/.h` | Screen brightness management and power control |
| Battery Service | `eos_service_battery.c/.h` | Battery status monitoring and power management |
| Power Manager Service | `eos_service_pm.c/.h` | System power state and sleep management |
| Haptic Service | `eos_service_haptic.c/.h` | Haptic feedback control |
| Time Service | `eos_service_time.c/.h` | System time acquisition |
| Storage Service | `eos_service_storage.c/.h` | File system operations and JSON storage |
| Config Service | `eos_service_config.c/.h` | System configuration management |
| State Service | `eos_service_state.c/.h` | Runtime persistent state management |
| Log Service | `eos_log.c/.h` | Logging system |

### Service Naming Conventions

Service file naming: `eos_service_<service_name>.c/.h`

Service initialization API: `eos_service_<service_name>_init()`

Other APIs are unified as: `eos_<service_name>_<function_name>()`

## Device Framework

### Device Manager

The device manager is the **only path** for the upper layer to obtain device instances.

#### Supported Device Types

| Device Type | Device File | Description |
|------------|-------------|-------------|
| Sensor Device | `eos_dev_sensor.c/.h` | Multi-instance support, linked list management |
| Display Device | `eos_dev_display.c/.h` | Single instance |
| Battery Device | `eos_dev_battery.c/.h` | Single instance |
| Power Device | `eos_dev_power.c/.h` | Single instance |
| Time Device | `eos_dev_time.c/.h` | Single instance |
| Vibrator Device | `eos_dev_vibrator.c/.h` | Single instance |

#### Required Device Manager Capabilities

1. **Registration Function** (must be named `register`)
   - Input parameter is OPS pointer
   - Used for registering device instances

2. **Device Lookup Function**
   - Single instance devices provide `get_instance` or `get_default`
   - Multi-instance devices provide `find` and `find_by_type` APIs

3. **Get Device State** (`get_state`)
   - Used for querying current device state

4. **Device State Report** (`report`)
   - Called by driver layer to report device state changes

#### Forbidden Device Manager Implementations

1. PORT is forbidden; provide OPS for device control, weak definitions are forbidden
2. Business interfaces are forbidden (e.g., sampling frequency settings, mode switching, etc.)
3. Unregistration functions are forbidden
4. User data fields are forbidden

#### Basic Device Structure

```c
typedef enum {
    DEV_STATE_NONE = 0,   // Not exist / Unregistered
    DEV_STATE_READY,      // Initialized, available
    DEV_STATE_BUSY,       // In use
    DEV_STATE_ERROR,      // Error occurred
} eos_dev_state_t;

typedef struct {
    const eos_<device_name>_ops_t *ops;
    <private_info>
    eos_dev_state_t _state; // Private field
} eos_<device_name>_dev_t;
```

### Sensor Device

Sensor devices support multi-instance management, organized using linked lists.

#### Sensor Types

```c
typedef enum {
    EOS_SENSOR_TYPE_UNKNOWN = 0,
    EOS_SENSOR_TYPE_ACCE,       // Accelerometer
    EOS_SENSOR_TYPE_GYRO,       // Gyroscope
    EOS_SENSOR_TYPE_HR,         // Heart Rate Sensor
    EOS_SENSOR_TYPE_SPO2,       // SpO2 Sensor
    EOS_SENSOR_TYPE_LIGHT,      // Ambient Light Sensor
    EOS_SENSOR_TYPE_PROXIMITY,  // Proximity Sensor
    EOS_SENSOR_TYPE_ECG,        // ECG Sensor
    EOS_SENSOR_TYPE_TEMP,       // Temperature Sensor
    EOS_SENSOR_TYPE_MAG,        // Magnetometer
    EOS_SENSOR_TYPE_BARO,       // Barometer
    EOS_SENSOR_TYPE_CAP,        // Capacitance Sensor
    EOS_SENSOR_TYPE_STEP,       // Step Counter
    EOS_SENSOR_TYPE_MAX
} eos_sensor_type_t;
```

#### Sensor Data Structure

```c
typedef union {
    eos_sensor_data_acce_t acce;
    eos_sensor_data_gyro_t gyro;
    eos_sensor_data_mag_t mag;
    eos_sensor_data_temp_t temp;
    eos_sensor_data_baro_t baro;
    eos_sensor_data_light_t light;
    eos_sensor_data_proximity_t proximity;
    eos_sensor_data_hr_t hr;
    eos_sensor_data_spo2_t spo2;
    eos_sensor_data_ecg_t ecg;
    eos_sensor_data_cap_t cap;
    eos_sensor_data_step_t step;
    eos_sensor_data_battery_t battery;
} eos_sensor_data_t;

typedef struct {
    eos_sensor_type_t type;
    eos_sensor_data_t data;
    uint32_t timestamp;  // Obtained using eos_tick_get()
} eos_sensor_raw_data_t;
```

#### Sensor Data Structure Design Requirements

- Sensor name (for lookup)
- Sensor type
- Sensor state
- Sensor data cache (FIFO, implemented with ring buffer)
- Sensor event ID (auto-registered)
- Sensor read period (0 means no auto-read, in milliseconds)

## Device Control Interface (OPS)

OPS (Operations) is the portable interface provided downward, defined in `eos_dev_<device_name>.h`.

### OPS Design Principles

- Device layer does not provide read operations; data is pushed to service layer via `eos_sensor_notify()`
- Service layer manages FIFO and broadcasts to subscribers
- OPS return type should be `eos_result_t` or `bool`, simple operations can return `void`

### OPS Example (Sensor)

```c
typedef struct {
    void (*init)(eos_dev_sensor_t *dev);
    void (*deinit)(eos_dev_sensor_t *dev);
    void (*enable)(eos_dev_sensor_t *dev);
    void (*disable)(eos_dev_sensor_t *dev);
    void (*set_sample_rate)(eos_dev_sensor_t *dev, uint32_t hz);
    void (*get_sample_rate)(eos_dev_sensor_t *dev, uint32_t *hz);
} eos_dev_sensor_ops_t;
```

### Device Control Interface Constraints

- Other services are forbidden from directly calling this service's corresponding OPS
- Each device type can only be operated by its corresponding Service, not by other Services
- OPS should not contain report functions (report is provided by device manager)

## Sensor Data Flow

### Pull Mode (Synchronous)

- When calling the interface, data is immediately read from sensor data cache
- If no data available, returns empty or error code
- Does not affect sensor sampling behavior

### Push Mode (Asynchronous)

- Subscribe to sensor data by registering callback function
- Sensor service triggers callback at set frequency
- Each subscriber can independently configure expected data frequency
- Callback executes in non-interrupt context

### Data Report Flow

```
driver → sensor_report(type, data)
              ↓
         Fast Enqueue (interrupt-safe)
              ↓
         Write to Ring Buffer
              ↓
         Service Layer Scheduling
              ↓
         Callback Distribution
```

### Design Constraints

- Device layer is forbidden from directly calling upper layer callback functions
- All sensor data must first enter cache, then be distributed by service layer
- Services are forbidden from directly accessing sensor devices; must use service interface
- Interrupt context only allows data report operations

## Event System

### Event Registration

```c
eos_event_code_t eos_event_register_id(void);
```

Gets user-defined event ID, starting from `EOS_EVENT_LAST`.

### Event Subscribe and Publish

```c
// Subscribe to event
void eos_event_subscribe(eos_event_code_t event_id, eos_event_cb_t cb, void *user_data);

// Publish event
void eos_event_post(eos_event_code_t event_id, void *param, lv_obj_t *obj);
```

### Built-in Event Types

| Event Name | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| `EOS_EVENT_APP_UNINSTALLED` | Application has been uninstalled |
| `EOS_EVENT_APP_INSTALLED` | Application has been installed |
| `EOS_EVENT_SYSTEM_SLEEP` | System entered sleep |
| `EOS_EVENT_SYSTEM_DISPLAY_ON` | System awakened |
| `EOS_EVENT_SYSTEM_DISPLAY_AOD` | Always-on display mode |
| `EOS_EVENT_SYSTEM_CONFIG_UPDATE` | Configuration has been updated |
| `EOS_EVENT_SCRIPT_STARTED` | Script has started |
| `EOS_EVENT_SCRIPT_EXITED` | Script has exited |
| `EOS_EVENT_ACTIVITY_SCREEN_SWITCHED` | Page transition completed |
| `EOS_EVENT_LANGUAGE_CHANGED` | Language has been changed |

## FIFO Ring Buffer

FIFO is used for sensor data caching with statistics support.

### Key Features

- Write operations overwrite old data (when full)
- Supports statistics: write count, read count, overflow count, peak usage
- Thread-safe (critical section protection)

### Core API

```c
eos_fifo_t *eos_fifo_create(uint16_t capacity);
uint16_t eos_fifo_write(eos_fifo_t *fifo, const void *data, uint16_t size);
uint16_t eos_fifo_read(eos_fifo_t *fifo, void *buf, uint16_t size);
bool eos_fifo_is_empty(eos_fifo_t *fifo);
bool eos_fifo_is_full(eos_fifo_t *fifo);
void eos_fifo_get_stats(eos_fifo_t *fifo, eos_fifo_stats_t *stats);
```

## Logging System

The logging system adopts a listener-based pattern, supporting multiple listeners.

### Log Levels

```c
typedef enum {
    EOS_LOG_LEVEL_DEBUG = 0,
    EOS_LOG_LEVEL_INFO,
    EOS_LOG_LEVEL_WARN,
    EOS_LOG_LEVEL_ERROR
} eos_log_level_t;
```

### Log Macros

```c
#define EOS_LOG_D(fmt, ...)  // Debug
#define EOS_LOG_I(fmt, ...)  // Info
#define EOS_LOG_W(fmt, ...)  // Warning
#define EOS_LOG_E(fmt, ...)  // Error
```

### Listener Registration

```c
eos_log_listener_id_t eos_log_register_listener(
    const char *name,
    eos_log_listener_cb_t cb,
    void *user_data,
    uint8_t flags
);
```

## File Naming Conventions

| Type | Convention |
|-----|------------|
| Service File | `eos_service_<service_name>.c/.h` |
| Device File | `eos_dev_<device_name>.c/.h` |
| Service Initialization | `eos_service_<service_name>_init()` |
| Service Other APIs | `eos_<service_name>_<function_name>()` |

# Application Management Module

The application management module is responsible for the identity, discovery, installation, uninstallation, ordering, and launch coordination of installed applications. It does not own script Realms, nor does it directly drive Activity pages; these responsibilities belong to SPM and the Activity controller respectively.

## Application Model

Applications and watch faces use the same EPKG v1 container. The `package_type` in the package header determines installation dispatch, and the `id` in `manifest.json` is the stable key for runtime identity, installation directory, and Recent Apps. Application management completes preview, manifest reading, full validation, and unpacking through a unified package context. For the internal layout and field semantics of the installation package, see [EPKG v1 Installation Package Format](../../package_format); for the official project and packaging workflow, see [ElenixOS-Toolkit](../../../development/toolkit).

The installation process sequentially reads metadata, checks the API level and package type, fully validates the EPKG, unpacks to an installation directory named by ID, and updates the discovery results and ordering state. Preview only provides metadata and does not constitute full validation. Installation success or failure is expressed through result codes and system events; whether a directory appears is not used as the criterion for installation result.

## Installation and Uninstallation

When installing an application with the same ID, the existing installation content is handled according to replacement semantics; the application ID must not change due to a change in the package file name. Uninstallation must simultaneously handle the installation content, application data, and permission records, and publish an uninstallation event; after a successful installation, publish an installation event.

Package parsing, decompression buffers, manifest temporary information, and installation target paths each have independent release responsibilities. After closing the EPKG context, its header, file table, or file handles must not continue to be read.

## List, Ordering, and Launch

The application list is rediscovered by installation directory, and the ordering sequence is saved by the `app_order` configuration; uninstalled IDs are no longer valid ordering entries. Application management is responsible for stable identity and ordering, not for creating Activities or deciding page exit policies.

When opening a new script application, the application manager first establishes and enters the App Activity that hosts the loading UI, then requests SPM to synchronously run the script; `main.js` establishes the page content in the startup call stack. After a successful return, the Activity binds the program instance ID and engine generation. Recent Apps restoration reattaches the same instance without creating a parallel Realm. **Directly calling `script_engine` to launch an application is prohibited**.

## Programs and Recent Apps

When an application leaves the foreground, the Activity controller first detaches the application Activity sub-stack; Recent Apps then parks the program and page as `SUSPENDED`, or performs a full destruction. Recent Apps entries bind to the program instance ID and may save snapshots for return animations. After reaching the count or memory watermark, the system evicts entries through the per-instance stop path, while cleaning up the corresponding program and associated state.

Suspension retains the program instance and is not equivalent to exit. Sensor requirements, audio, timers, animations, and script callbacks are handled according to the program suspend/resume policy; resources that continue to be retained have explicit owners and recovery paths.

## Architectural Constraints

- The application ID is a stable key; package paths, display names, or package file names must not be used in its place.
- SPM is the sole owner of the script program lifecycle; the application manager must not directly operate the Script Engine Core, nor directly call `script_engine` to launch an application.
- Two unterminated script programs with the same application ID must not exist simultaneously.
- The cleanup of Activities, Recent Apps, and SPM must be completed as a set, and must not produce "Recent Apps entries without a program" or "script programs still referencing an old View".
- The current format only accepts EPKG v1; the legacy EAPK/EWPK compatibility paths and the installation flow distinguished by magic are deprecated.

For the application-perspective Pull/Push, synchronous/asynchronous, and lifecycle contracts, see [Application and Framework Contract](../../application_contract); for platform-side registration and reporting methods, see [Platform/Vendor Contract](../../platform_contract).

# Recent Apps

Recent Apps is the app switcher and also the retained registry of suspended script apps. It stores app IDs, App Activity, page state, snapshots, and resource estimates in most-recently-used order.

## Entry and Behavior

A long press of the crown opens Recent Apps; another long press on the Recent Apps page returns to the previous page. A short press of the crown enters the app list from the watch face, and performs back on ordinary pages. Selecting a Recent Apps card restores the corresponding app rather than starting a brand-new script context.

## Suspension and Resumption

When an app is suspended, the system retains the resumable Activity substack and page state, and pauses the program's script callback resources. On resumption, pages are reattached, and then timers and animations are resumed according to configuration:

| Resource | Resumption strategy |
|---|---|
| Timer | Execute one missed callback, execute all missed callbacks (up to 10 catch-up firings), or skip missed callbacks and restart the timer |
| Animation | Continue from the paused position, or jump to the end state |

The Simulator by default fires at most one catch-up callback for timers that expired during suspension, and lets animations continue from the paused position.`EOS_RECENT_APPS_TIMER_STRATEGY`and`EOS_RECENT_APPS_ANIM_STRATEGY`can be adjusted in the Recent Apps group of [the kernel configuration system](../../../development/kconfig)].

During suspension, whether a timer keeps running depends on its resumption strategy. Logic that requires accurate time can re-read the system time upon resumption.

## Count and Eviction

By default, up to 3 entries are retained, with an estimated memory high-water mark of 2.5 MiB; both can be adjusted via Kconfig. Once the count or memory high-water mark is exceeded, the system evicts entries in least-recently-used order. When an entry is evicted, the corresponding app is fully stopped, and its associated state such as the card, script resources, Activity, and snapshot is cleaned up as well.

App uninstallation, script engine reset, and app stop also remove the corresponding Recent Apps entry. Entries that have already been evicted cannot be restored.

Parking only describes the program/page retention policy; it does not automatically release the user_data or subscriptions of a given native Service consumer. For explicit cleanup responsibilities on the app side, see [the Application contract](../../application_contract).

# Hardware Layer

The hardware layer is the display, input, sensor, storage, audio, and power hardware that device drivers actually control. ElenixOS's upper-layer APIs do not directly describe a specific chip; the platform provides available capabilities through drivers and device operation tables.

Different platforms may provide different device implementations and capabilities; a software device implementation cannot prove that a certain feature is supported by specific hardware. Display dimensions, input methods, and device characteristics are defined by the corresponding platform and device.

Porting to real hardware requires implementing the corresponding operations for the supported devices and registering them before service initialization. Unimplemented device capabilities should remain unavailable, and services should return errors or capability status; upper layers must not assume that functionality exists based on the hardware layer's intended design.

# Event Bus

The event bus synchronously broadcasts system state changes by event identifier. It is used to notify about application installation, system power and display status, script lifecycle, page switching, and language changes; it is not an asynchronous message queue, nor does it replace the Activity stack or LVGL widget events.

## Publish and Subscribe

Modules can subscribe to the events they need and unsubscribe when notifications are no longer required. Subscriptions can be associated with an object to manage the subscription lifecycle, but the associated object does not turn a global broadcast into a targeted message.

Event callbacks execute synchronously during the publish process and inherit the thread/task/interrupt context of the publisher; the Event Bus does not automatically deliver them to the LVGL main loop. Therefore, when a publisher publishes from an ISR, all subscribers may also execute within the ISR. When GUI/file/script operations are needed, callbacks should copy the necessary data and hand it off to the Dispatcher for deferred processing, or the publisher itself should defer before publishing.

The `param` provided by the publisher and the associated object are both borrowed resources: callbacks may only use them within the lifetime guaranteed by the owner; if they need to be retained across callbacks, the subscriber must copy the data or establish an explicit ownership relationship. Events such as battery changes and page switches convey service/page state, not ownership of the state object.

A callback may request to unsubscribe; if a broadcast is in progress, the actual node cleanup is deferred to a safe point. Modules should clean up associated subscriptions when the owner is destroyed to prevent callbacks from continuing to access expired objects.

Event identifiers registered at runtime are only valid within the current process instance and should not be saved as persistent protocol numbers.

The Event Bus only defines a synchronous broadcast protocol; it does not provide deferred execution, thread-safe callbacks, or background queue semantics. For cross-context submission, see [Task Scheduler](../scheduler/dispatcher).

# Task Dispatcher

The task dispatcher submits short tasks from other threads or interrupt contexts to the system main loop, processing them in sequence in a context suitable for executing UI and system logic. It is a deferred execution queue across contexts, not a general-purpose thread scheduler.

## Queue and Execution

The dispatcher uses a circular queue protected by a critical section to store callbacks and their user data. When queue space is insufficient, it attempts to expand; memory allocation failure may cause new tasks to be lost. Tasks in the queue are processed by the main loop in submission order, and the queue protection is released during callback execution so that other contexts can continue submitting work.

## Usage Boundaries

Submitters should keep callbacks short and ensure that user data remains valid until the task executes. In interrupts, only collect the necessary information and submit follow-up work; tasks that need to operate on LVGL must execute in the GUI main loop. The queue does not provide task priorities, cancellation, or reliable persistence guarantees.
