# Watchface System

The watchface is the system's root page. Both the built-in watchface and JavaScript watchfaces are displayed through the root Activity and are not pushed onto the Activity stack as ordinary pages; their scripts and Views are still managed by their respective runtime lifecycles.

## Watchface Model

Current watchface installation and application installation share EPKG v1. The package header's `package_type` must be Watch Face, and the manifest's `id`, API level, and permission declarations determine runtime identity and compatibility. The watchface manager should not maintain a second set of package parsing or unpacking logic. For the in-package structure, see [EPKG v1 Package Format](../../package_format); the Toolkit can build existing watchface projects, but currently does not provide Watchface project initialization, see [ElenixOS-Toolkit](../../../development/toolkit) for details.

The watchface list includes the built-in fallback watchface. The fallback watchface is a system resource, not an installable item that can be uninstalled like an ordinary package; only installed JS watchfaces come from the watchface installation directory. The default watchface ID is determined by system configuration.

## Switching and Lifecycle

The watchface manager coordinates watchface switching through SPM's start, resume, and stop flows, and replaces the root Activity; its call boundary with `script_engine` is managed by SPM. The old watchface's Activity, View, script Realm, SNI callbacks, and watchface components all become invalid during the replacement flow. After switching completes, the caller re-acquires the current root object from the root Activity interface; the old root pointer becomes invalid with the replacement.

When opening an application, the current JS watchface can enter a suspended state; when returning to the watchface, the same program instance is resumed. Switching watchfaces, uninstalling watchfaces, Recent Apps eviction, or engine reset all perform a full destruction, and the old watchface no longer exists as a resumable page.

## Data, Components, and Page Ownership

JS watchfaces use `main.js` as the entry point and create pages through the system interfaces exposed by SNI. The Activity/View determines the lifecycle of the page and the LVGL object tree; the watchface script does not own the root Activity.

Data and drawing components are two distinct extension boundaries. `eos.metric` maps existing service state to semantic values; `eos.ww` exposes reusable native LVGL watchface controls to scripts. A component can bind to an existing Metric, or the script can pass read results into the component. In this way, components focus on presentation, while data services focus on units, validity, expiration state, and source.

Metric currently uses static semantic mapping and has no dynamically registerable Provider plugin model. Adding a new watchface component that consumes an existing Metric does not require changing the sensor or Metric service; adding new semantic data requires extending the Metric mapping and SNI exposure. If the data comes from new hardware, it should first pass through the corresponding device/service boundary, and watchface components should not access drivers directly.

The LVGL handles returned by watchface components belong to their parent View and the root Activity; when the object tree is destroyed, the component's timers, callbacks, and internal resources must also become invalid in sync. The resources accessible to scripts are still limited to the interfaces registered with SNI, and after the root Activity is replaced, all old handles expire.

## Architecture Constraints

- The watchface is the root Activity and must not fake a second root page through the ordinary page stack API.
- Watchface start, resume, and stop are all managed by SPM; the watchface manager does not directly call `script_engine` to create or start a script context.
- Watchface switching must handle the ownership of the root Activity, View, script program, and watchface-specific components simultaneously.
- The built-in fallback watchface cannot be deleted as an ordinary installable package, and the configuration must not point to a watchface ID that no longer exists.
- Watchface packages must first pass complete EPKG v1 validation before unpacking and loading scripts; a successful preview does not mean it is runnable.
- New code should use root Activity semantics to access the current watchface and should not rely on deprecated dedicated getters.

For watchface consumers and the SPM lifecycle, see [Application Contract](../../application_contract); for platform data sources, see [Platform/Vendor Contract](../../platform_contract); for data mapping, SNI lifecycle, and UI hierarchy, see [Metric](../../services/metric), [SNI](../../script_engine/sni), and [UI](../../ui) respectively.

# Runtime

The runtime combines platform initialization, system services, Activity pages, and script programs. It is not a thin wrapper for "scripts calling C functions," but rather a lifecycle coordination layer for programs, Realms, pages, and native resources.

## Runtime Model

At startup, platform display/input and device registration are established first, then system services are initialized, and finally the root Activity, script runtime, and applications/watchfaces are started. When platform capabilities are insufficient, this is expressed upward through device state, capability queries, or service return codes; the startup process must not assume that all platforms provide the same capabilities.

Script programs, Activities, and Views are three distinct ownership layers:

- SPM owns script programs, JavaScript Realms, SNI contexts, and script callbacks.
- The Activity controller owns the page stack, root Activity, page Views, and transitions.
- LVGL owns child controls in the object tree; deleting a parent object may cascade-delete them.

SPM is the sole entry point for the script program lifecycle. Upper-layer application/watchface managers **are prohibited from directly calling `script_engine` to start applications or watchfaces**, and must not bypass SPM to operate the Script Engine Core; starting, resuming, suspending, and stopping must all be done through SPM's application/watchface management interfaces. Only one unterminated program instance is allowed per application ID; the instance ID links the program, Activity, and Recent Apps record together.

## Program and Page States

Program states are `ACTIVE`, `SUSPENDED`, `STOPPING`, or `TERMINATED`. Suspension means the program can still be resumed, typically preserving the Realm, page sub-stack, and Recent Apps snapshot; only eviction, uninstallation, root watchface replacement, or a fatal engine error leads to a full stop.

Activities use their own page states and exit policies. Page transitions explicitly choose to preserve, destroy, or park, rather than letting the caller modify a long-lived destroy/suspend flag. Ordinary Activities cannot be directly destroyed by arbitrary callers; the root Activity is managed by the root replacement process.

## Callbacks, Execution Context, and Engine Reset

SNI callbacks record the owner program and engine generation. Before entering a callback, it must be confirmed that the program is still active, the context is not suspended, and the generation has not changed; the owner Realm is entered before calling JS. After an LVGL object is deleted or the engine is reset, old callbacks, old handles, and old native pointers all become invalid.

A fatal engine error saves the error context, destroys the affected SPM program and cleans up the Recent Apps entry, and then the Script Engine Core rebuilds the JerryScript heap within the current OS process. A Core rebuild does not mean that all crashed programs automatically restart: Applications and JavaScript Watchfaces enter the error-handling/user-restart path; Console fatal automatically rebuilds the Watchface and restarts the previous script application according to recovery conditions. Old pages, Views, and JS objects become invalid with the old engine generation; for the capture and rebuild order and the recovery paths for each type, see [Script Engine Overview](./script_engine_overview).

## Threading and Invocation Constraints

The runtime main loop executes Activity/LVGL operations, LVGL timers, and the SNI/JS callbacks dispatched by those timers. The `main.js` of a newly started application is executed synchronously by SPM, which occupies the main loop call that initiated the start; the loading screen does not let the script run in parallel.

The Event Bus itself does not switch threads or queue: `eos_event_post` synchronously invokes subscribers in the publisher's context. Sensor `eos_sensor_notify` also synchronously invokes Native subscribers in the publisher's context; Battery data changes emit events synchronously within the `eos_battery_report_raw` call stack. They cannot all be treated as GUI main loop callbacks. If a platform ISR/device thread wants to trigger a chain that may access LVGL, the file system, or scripts, it should first defer to the appropriate context through the Dispatcher or the target Service's thread-safe entry point; data passed across threads must be copied or kept valid before being queued.

Even if a callback is dispatched by a timer/Dispatcher, it still executes synchronously within the Core call stack and should be short and non-blocking. Only the callback's explicit scheduling boundary can indicate which context it runs in; asynchronous or thread-safe behavior cannot be inferred from the name `callback`.

## Runtime Constraints

- After an Activity/View is destroyed, all related C pointers and script handles must be considered invalid.
- Script resource release must be performed by the owning SPM/SNI context; applications cannot bypass system resource lifecycle through JS reference counting.
- When a program is suspended, its timers, animations, and script callbacks are paused or resumed according to the Recent Apps recovery policy; no arbitrary JS continues to execute while suspended.
- New callbacks must be bound to an explicit owner, generation, and cancellation/deletion path; ownership cannot be guessed from a global current-program.

# JavaScript Programs and Runtime Constraints

ElenixOS applications and watchfaces can be implemented with JavaScript scripts. Scripts run in the JavaScript engine provided by the system, accessing ElenixOS capabilities through `eos` and creating and manipulating LVGL objects through `lv`.

## Script Package Entry

A script package should contain at least the `manifest.json` required by the runtime and an entry script. The entry file name for applications and watchfaces is `main.js`. The package's API compatibility is declared by `minApiLevel` and `targetApiLevel`; when `minApiLevel` is higher than the current system API level, the application will not start.

The manifest provides the script's identity, display information, API compatibility range, and optional permission declarations. The system checks the compatibility range; unrecognized permissions will not grant capabilities.

## Runtime Constraints

- **Directly calling `script_engine` to start an application or watchface is prohibited.** Application/watchface startup, resume, suspend, and stop must be managed through SPM; the script engine is merely the execution layer used by SPM.
- Scripts execute in the system event loop; long synchronous work or blocking waits will occupy the event loop and delay other work.
- The current script context only provides the two system API namespaces `eos` and `lv`.
- LVGL/ElenixOS objects visible to JS are handles managed by the runtime. After the owning Activity, View, or native object is destroyed, the original handle can no longer be used.
- Script exceptions, parse failures, module link failures, unresponsiveness, and engine crashes are categorized and handled by the runtime; legacy internal error constants do not constitute an application interface.
- Script callbacks should return as soon as possible. When deferred processing is needed, the timing or event mechanisms provided by the runtime should be used.

## Lifecycle

A script application creates a runtime context and executes the entry on startup; when switching to another page, the application can be suspended, and when returning to the application, the same context is resumed. Recent Apps retains a limited number of suspended applications; when the memory watermark or count limit is reached, the least recently used application is fully stopped and its context released.

A script watchface runs as the root Activity. When an application is opened, the watchface pauses, and when returning to the watchface, it resumes; when switching watchfaces, uninstalling a watchface, or resetting the engine, the old watchface is destroyed.

# Platform / Vendor Porting Contract

Platform porters implement the port/device operations declared by Core and register available devices before consumer services start. Core already provides device state, service policies, data caching, unit semantics, application APIs, and lifecycle management; Vendor provides chip access, board-level conversion, interrupt/DMA/RTOS glue, and non-portable HAL. Board-level implementations should not duplicate service policies, nor expose raw driver interfaces to applications.

## Startup and Registration Protocol

Core does not have a unified`port_init`, generic device`init/deinit`, or runtime hot-plug protocol covering all Vendors. Platform integration is responsible for preparing infrastructure and devices, then initializing services that depend on these devices, and finally entering Core initialization and the main loop.```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Host as Platform Integration
    participant Port as Vendor Port
    participant Device as Device Registry
    participant Service as OS Service
    participant Core as eos_init / Main Loop

    Host->>Port: 初始化时钟、显示/输入、FS、线程/临界区
    Port->>Device: 注册已实现的设备操作与能力
    Host->>Service: 初始化依赖设备的服务
    Host->>Core: eos_init()
    loop 每次系统循环
        Host->>Core: eos_main_loop()
    end
```Device registration must precede initialization of services that bind device instances. Sensor Service in particular requires explicit initialization: currently`eos_init()`does not call it, and platform integration must initialize the service after sensor registration and before Sensor API usage. When Sensor Service initializes, it binds the current default device of each type to the service instance; devices registered afterward will not automatically be taken over by that instance. There is also currently no unified deregistration, replacement, failover, or device hot-plug path.

Device initialization failure does not necessarily prevent system startup: currently`eos_init()`calls Battery Service initialization but does not check its failure result, while Sensor Service is initialized separately by the integration project. Core can still run without a battery, but battery status is invalid; without sensors, corresponding requirements or reads fail, or there are no samples. Therefore,`eos_init()`returning only indicates that the initialization process completed, not that all device services are available; the platform checks initialization results and capabilities as needed for the target product.

Operation tables for different device types are not a unified template. Successful registration means Core saved the implementation entry point, not that the device has actually started, is available, or that subsequent operations will necessarily succeed. Vendor should keep the operation table and its referenced state valid for at least the entire registration period; currently device registration has no paired generic deregistration protocol.

## Control Direction, Data Direction, and Implementation Responsibility

| Capability | Core-initiated control requests | Data / status returned by Vendor | Platform responsibility and optional capabilities |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sensor | Sensor Service calls enable/disable and set-rate according to aggregated demands; effective operation changes only when demand reaches zero or power policy changes. | Vendor delivers each sample to the service with common type, unit, coordinate system, and monotonic timestamp since boot; the service copies samples, updates FIFO/latest, and broadcasts synchronously. |`init/deinit`are also in the operation table, but the current Service does not call them; the target port is responsible for hardware initialization/shutdown after registration. Multiple instances are allowed to register, but the service currently fixes one default instance selected at initialization for each type, with no runtime priority or failover. |
| Battery | Battery Service calls`request_update`at initialization and when the LVGL timer expires; this call occurs in the Core calling context, and Vendor should return quickly and move slow reads to its own safe execution context. | Vendor obtains percentage, voltage, current, and charging status, then calls Core to report; Core updates valid status, history, and change events. Change events are broadcast synchronously in the calling context of`report_raw`. | Battery percentage must come from a reliable platform value; Core does not infer it from voltage on behalf of Vendor. When there is no valid report, applications read an invalid status. If reported from an ISR, all event subscribers also execute synchronously in that context, and they cannot be assumed to be in the UI main loop. |
| Display / Power | Display and PM services call registered brightness and power operations; calls are initiated synchronously in the service path. | Device status is reported by the platform via the device status interface; PM events represent Core software state changes. | LVGL display driver, scanout, and pointer/encoder input are provided by platform graphics/HAL integration. Display device ops are not a framebuffer output API. Some display operations have no unified error return; PM software state cannot be treated as hardware confirmation. |
| Speaker | Audio Player synchronously opens sample format, borrows output buffer, submits PCM, pauses/resumes/stops. | The speaker implementation consumes submitted PCM; playback progress, drain, and EOF notifications are optional ops. | The speaker is independent of the microphone and can be missing separately. Which PCM sample rates/channels/bit depths are supported is indicated by whether the device reports success; Core does not provide generic resampling. |
| Microphone | Audio Service opens format, hands the shared ring buffer to the device, starts/stops DMA, and reads the write cursor. | Vendor produces PCM into the shared buffer, and the Service consumes and writes to the target file. | The buffer is created by the Service and released after closing the device and stopping DMA; Vendor must not continue writing after stopping. Optional initialization, gain, and other capabilities cannot be assumed to exist. |
| Time | Time Service performs synchronous reads on the device. | Vendor returns the current date-time value. | Core does not specify the RTC chip, time calibration source, or timezone source; the target platform must provide data conforming to the common date-time representation. |
| Haptic | Haptic Service maps feedback intent to device intensity and on/off. | Currently only one-way control exists; there is no vibration sample stream that applications can subscribe to. | The on/off operation is void; the current Service has no per-pulse success/failure confirmation, and no complete missing-device capability API. Applications cannot confirm that physical feedback actually occurred. |
| Input | The platform registers LVGL display/indev at startup; knob and key adapters report physical actions to the Core input path. | Pointer events enter LVGL indev; crown/side keys enter Crown/Chrome/PM through their respective input entry points. | This is not a unified input Provider or Event Bus protocol. Touch, crown knob, crown key, and side key have different delivery paths; only inputs available on the current target need to be registered. |
| Storage | Core/Service performs synchronous file, directory, and path operations on the filesystem port. | The filesystem returns content, handles, and error codes. | The platform provides the actual filesystem and an optional virtual root; this root mapping is not an application isolation policy. Caller path restrictions are implemented in higher-layer APIs. |

This table describes directions and does not define a lifecycle common to all devices: Battery is requested by Core and reported by Vendor; Sensor has sampling demands issued by Core and samples pushed by Vendor; Time is pulled by Core; audio includes both Core control and continuous PCM production/consumption. Porting implementations follow the corresponding device contract, and each device retains its Push/Pull model.

## Sensor Data Protocol```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Consumer as Native Consumer
    participant Service as Sensor Service
    participant Device as Sensor Device
    participant Vendor as HAL / Sensor Driver

    Consumer->>Service: 建立订阅或采样需求
    Service->>Device: 需求聚合后的 enable / set-rate
    Device->>Vendor: 调用注册的操作
    Vendor-->>Service: 上报标准样本和采集时间戳
    Service->>Service: 复制、限速、缓存 FIFO/latest
    Service-->>Consumer: 同步 Push 回调
    Consumer->>Service: 取消订阅 / 释放需求
    Service->>Device: 重算所有剩余需求
```Sensors are required to report in the units and coordinates defined by the Core common data contract; timestamps are monotonic milliseconds since platform boot, not UTC.`eos_sensor_notify`copies the input parameters, but then synchronously executes consumer callbacks in the caller's context, and the sample pointer is valid only until the callback returns. Therefore, samples obtained from an ISR must first be delivered to a task or main loop that can safely run Core/consumer callbacks, and then the notification entry point is called. The hardware FIFO capabilities listed in the sensor device header are currently not wired and consumed by Sensor Service; the platform should read the hardware FIFO itself and report sample by sample, unless the current target integration separately implements the complete path.

Reporting identifies samples by Sensor Type, without a registered device name or instance ID; the Service cannot distinguish multiple sources of the same type at notification time. Therefore, current multi-instance registration is mainly used for device lookup and does not constitute aggregation of multiple Providers of the same type. One Sensor Type should have the default instance bound by the Service as the active source.

The effective period is the shortest period among all Native subscriptions, algorithm requests, and compatible demands, further limited by the minimum interval policy of the power mode; it is not a hardware ODR guarantee. The frequency that Sensor Service sends to the device is obtained by integer conversion and may be limited by the device's own discrete frequencies. Releasing a demand ID only removes that consumer and must not directly disable the device; Core disables the default device only when remaining demand is zero or policy prohibits enabling.

## Capabilities, State, and Fault Propagation

- Required/optional operations are defined separately by each device type; some registration entry points validate required operations, while others only validate the registration object.`NULL`indicates unsupported only when that type is explicitly marked optional; there is no unified validator. Optional operations are handled by the Service according to defined fallback/error paths and are not indicated as supported by silent success.
- Device state distinguishes unregistered, ready, busy, and error, but how each type changes state is defined by its contract; there is no global device state machine or automatic reconnection mechanism.
- Synchronous device operations can return errors and be mapped by the Service; asynchronous data sources propagate results through reported values, validity, or state changes. Vendor should not submit seemingly valid zero samples on error.
- Sensor data publication and Battery reports synchronously enter Core consumer/event callbacks. Interrupts only complete acquisition and queuing; if consumers may access LVGL, the filesystem, or JS, publication must be executed in an appropriate task context.
- LVGL pointer, display refresh, touch, crown, and side key initialization belong to the platform GUI/HAL path;`eos_dev_display`device operation tables do not cover these responsibilities.

Different devices currently have different strengths of error propagation, and the system has no unified confirmation model:

| Path | Currently observable result | Current limitation |
|---|---|---|
| Sensor | Demand acquisition can report no device, invalid state, etc.; Vendor can report Device status; invalid samples are reflected in no samples/timestamps. | enable/disable/set-rate operations are void; the notification entry point ignores uninitialized, uncached, or illegal type data, with no per-sample error receipt. |
| Battery | The Service retains invalid status; after receiving a qualified report, it updates the snapshot and emits change events according to thresholds. |`request_update`is void; there is no unified request ID, failure callback, or timeout event. |
| Display / Vibrator | Registration status and current Service requests are observable. | The main physical action operations are void; there is no per-operation hardware completion/failure confirmation. |
| Power | Device`set_power`has a return value. | PM Service currently ignores this return value and does not roll back the updated software state; failures do not become a unified hardware error that applications can subscribe to. |
| Speaker / Microphone | Operations can return synchronous results; Audio Service maps startup-phase failures to service results. | Asynchronous device failures after playback/recording starts have no unified completion error event. |
| File system | Each file operation returns a port/service result or an invalid handle. | The result represents that file operation, not that a higher-layer application transaction was atomically committed. |

Vendor should accurately implement the defined reporting paths and must not fake a "hardware success" signal when there is no confirmation channel. If a capability requires reliable asynchronous confirmation, a contract with request ownership, completion/failure, and cancellation semantics should first be established for that Device/Service.

## Contracts Not Yet Defined by Current Interfaces

Platform porting needs to verify buffer lifecycle and error semantics. The current speaker`borrow`/`enqueue`operations expose the buffer acquisition and submission steps, but the device header does not fully define ownership transfer or reuse timing of the buffer after submission; this semantics has not yet formed a cross-platform guarantee. The target port and its tests can explicitly verify current implementation behavior, but until a stable public guarantee is formed, this item remains undefined behavior.

Similarly, most Display hardware operations have no return value, and PM Service first updates Core software state and then requests the power device; the software state or events observed by applications do not prove that physical power switching succeeded. Device status and target platform diagnostics are used to observe actual faults, and Core does not provide hardware success confirmation.

# Object

`lv.obj` is the base class for most script controls. It requires a parent object:

```js
const obj = new lv.obj(eos.view.active());
obj.setSize(100, 100);
obj.align(lv.ALIGN_CENTER, 0, 0);
obj.addFlag(lv.OBJ_FLAG_CLICKABLE);
```

The common interface covers position and size (`setPos`, `setSize`, `setX`, `setY`), layout (`align`, `alignTo`, flex/grid), parent-child relationships, flags, styles, events, and deletion. Deleting an object tree may cascade-delete child objects, so after deleting a parent object all child handles must be considered invalid.

Events are registered via `addEventCb(callback, code, userData)`, can be canceled with `removeEventCb` or `removeEventCbWithUserData`, or sent with `sendEvent`. Callbacks execute synchronously in the LVGL context; blocking will delay other work in that context, and handles to deleted objects are already invalid.

# Battery Service

The battery service is a combination of pull requests and push reports: the Service calls the device's `request_update` according to initialization/timer policy, and the Vendor reports data after obtaining it; the Service validates the percentage, updates the state snapshot/history, and synchronously publishes events on meaningful changes. The percentage reported by the platform device is the primary source of battery level; Core does not derive battery level from voltage on behalf of the Vendor at the application layer or in the Service.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Service as Battery Service
    participant Vendor as Battery Port
    participant App as Framework Consumer
    Service->>Vendor: request_update
    Note right of Vendor: Read hardware, may complete asynchronously
    Vendor-->>Service: report raw state
    Service->>Service: Validate and update valid state/history
    Service-->>App: State change event (synchronous)
    App->>Service: pull current state
```

## Sampling Policy

The service automatically selects normal, low power, and charging modes based on the battery level when not charging and the charging status. The default policies are as follows:

| Mode | Entry Condition | Request Interval | Battery Event Threshold |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Normal | Not charging and battery level above 20% | 60 seconds | 1 percentage point |
| Low Power | Not charging and battery level at or below 20% | 300 seconds | 2 percentage points |
| Charging | Charging | 5 seconds | 1 percentage point |

The Service requests an update immediately upon initialization, after which an LVGL timer requests periodically according to the current mode. The device's `request_update` has no synchronous read return value; the state is only updated after the device reports. Events are triggered according to the thresholds in the table above or on charging status changes, and are not broadcast on every poll. The mode intervals and thresholds are currently fixed in the Battery Service implementation and are not Kconfig options.

## State and Notifications

Consumers can pull the current snapshot or subscribe to battery level/charging changes. Service events are triggered by change thresholds rather than broadcast on every sample. When there is no valid device reading yet, the state remains invalid, and default values do not represent real measurements. The device request entry point does not return sampling results; a successful initialization also does not mean the first valid value has been received.

The service also aggregates capacity, cycle count, and battery level change history; the change history stores up to 128 entries, overwriting the oldest entry when full, and identical consecutive battery level/charging states are not recorded repeatedly. The history count and entries are read via the service API, and consumers should not directly modify the internal records.

Device registration and `request_update` are part of the platform-side contract; after the update report completes, events execute synchronously in the context of the report call. When the platform reports from an ISR, all battery event subscribers also run synchronously in that ISR context, so this path is only suitable when the entire downstream callback chain has been confirmed to be executable in interrupt context; in other cases, the platform defers to an appropriate task/Core context first. For general responsibilities, see [Platform/Vendor Contract](../../platform_contract) and [Application Contract](../../application_contract).

# Configuration Service

The configuration service manages system-level settings and persists them as JSON. Configuration items cover device and language, display and power, audio and haptics, watchface and app ordering, and security options. System modules access them through typed configuration and should not parse or rewrite the system configuration file themselves.

When reading a configuration item that is missing or has a type mismatch, the caller-provided default value is used. Dynamic strings and JSON trees are freed by the caller according to their respective resource rules. Development debug options may also be stored as ordinary configuration data and do not thereby become compile-time configuration.

Script configuration and system configuration are isolated from each other and are stored in the data directory of the corresponding app or watchface; system-level configuration is not part of the script configuration boundary.

The configuration service is a synchronous Core-owned settings snapshot, and when a key is missing the reader provides the default semantics; it is not a real-time device data subscription. JS `eos.config` writes to the corresponding app/watchface configuration location based on the current script identity, whereas the generic Storage API does not automatically apply this identity isolation. For the calling layer, see [Application Contract](../../application_contract).

# Audio Service

The Audio Service coordinates playback control, format decoding, speaker output, and microphone recording. Applications express playback or recording intent through the service; the service manages player state and device access, and does not let applications directly control the Codec or platform audio ports.

## Playback Chain and Replaceable Decoders

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Client[System or Application] --> Service[Audio Service]
    Service --> Player[Player]
    Player -->|probe source| Registry[Decoder Registry]
    Registry -->|recognized decoder| Player
    Player -->|PCM buffer and format| Speaker[Speaker Device]
    Speaker --> Port[Platform Output Implementation]
```

A Decoder parses an input source into PCM frames consumable by the player. Registry entries provide the player with source probing, open, read, close, and optional seek capabilities; the Player manages generic playback state and submits decoded buffers to the speaker device. This separates Codec file-format logic from pause, resume, seek, and the output queue.

The Decoder registry is the format extension point; the Player's scheduling logic calls probes in registration order and uses the first Decoder that accepts the source. The current WAV Decoder is registered in the Audio Service initialization path, and overlapping probes create a selection-order dependency. An opened playback descriptor borrows the Decoder registry node until the corresponding close completes; Core currently has no active reference counting or safe hot-unload protocol.

After opening the Decoder, playback hands its sample rate, channel count, and bit depth to the speaker device. The Player does not take on Codec-specific processing, and Core has no generic PCM transcoding layer; startup succeeds when the device accepts the format and fails when it does not.

## Feed and Platform Output

Playback does not synchronously read the entire audio in the caller's startup path; the feed clock subsequently drives buffer filling. The current default feed uses an LVGL timer, so callbacks execute in the LVGL main loop. Platforms can replace the feed implementation to hook into RTOS/DMA clocks, and the replacement does not change the data contract between Decoder and Player. The Player's supply callback reads the file, decodes, and submits speaker buffers; implementations using an ISR feed need to defer these operations to a context that can execute them, or provide corresponding interrupt-safe capabilities. The default feed is not a background worker thread.

The speaker device provides capabilities such as opening a format, borrowing/submitting buffers, pause/resume, stop, and playback progress through typed operations. Devices and ports may be missing or may not support a particular operation, and the Audio Service returns the corresponding failure to the caller. The playback instance is held uniformly by the service, and callers do not own the player's internal state.

## Request, Continuous Execution, and Stop

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Application / Framework
    participant Service as Audio Service
    participant Player
    participant Decoder as Decoder
    participant Speaker as Speaker Device

    App->>Service: play(path)
    Service->>Speaker: check device availability
    Service->>Player: probe and open Decoder
    Player->>Decoder: probe / open
    Player->>Speaker: open(format)
    Service-->>App: synchronously return startup result
    loop During playback
        Player->>Decoder: read PCM
        Player->>Speaker: borrow / enqueue
    end
    App->>Service: pause / stop
    Service->>Player: stop supplying data or close playback
    Player->>Player: delete feed, prevent further supply
    Player->>Speaker: pause / stop
    Player->>Decoder: close
```

A synchronous success from `play` only means the Decoder and speaker have accepted startup; subsequent file reads, decoding, and PCM consumption continue. The default feed supplies data in the LVGL timer callback, so a single file read or Decoder block occupies the main loop. Failure is returned during startup when no Decoder is found, the device is missing, the format is not accepted, or resources are insufficient; asynchronous port failures after startup have no unified playback error event contract. If the speaker provides a drain query, the Player waits for queued samples to be exhausted before ending naturally; without that capability, Core cannot prove that the last sample has been physically output.

Pause pauses data supply and preserves Decoder/player state; stop deletes the feed, stops the speaker, and closes the Decoder. The service holds a copy of the playback source path for seek/reopen, but the `src` pointer exposed by the Decoder descriptor has no documented borrow period in the public interface. The current WAV implementation establishes its own file handle when opening the file; a new Decoder that needs to continue using source data after `open` returns should copy/hold it itself, and cannot rely on the caller's temporary string remaining valid.

## Recording, Volume, and Configuration

Microphone recording is managed by the Audio Service: the service creates a DMA-shared ring buffer and hands it to the microphone device, periodically reads the device's write cursor, handles buffer wrap-around, and writes new samples to a WAV file. The current format is fixed at 16 kHz, mono, 16-bit PCM. On stop, the service reads the unread interval at the cursor once more, then stops and closes the microphone, backfills the WAV length, and frees the buffer. Speaker and recording input are separate device capabilities; the presence of a speaker does not imply the presence of a microphone.

Volume and mute are saved by the service and applied to the speaker; mute does not overwrite the saved volume value. Playback still reads and decodes source data to advance the playback position and end naturally, and only fills the PCM buffer submitted this time with zeros; after unmuting, the original volume takes effect again. The specific volume control granularity and hardware behavior depend on device capabilities.

## Ownership and Extension Constraints

- Decoder registry entries are established during service initialization and held by the registry; the Decoder descriptor opened for playback and its source resources are closed by the Player on the end path.
- New formats are extended through Decoder registration; format probing and decoding are not implemented in the Audio Service or the speaker device.
- Platform speaker and microphone implementations provide device operations and do not hold application playback policy or page lifecycle.
- The feed implementation can be replaced by the platform; the execution context of the supply callback and buffer ownership determine the callable scope of LVGL, the script runtime, and speaker operations.
- The player instance is held by the Audio Service, and the application-side control entry point is the Audio Service API.
- The public device header does not fully define buffer ownership and reuse timing after Speaker `borrow`/`enqueue`, so these operations have no cross-platform unified guarantee.

For upper-layer start/stop and asynchronous completion semantics, see [Application Contract](../../application_contract); for device registration and Vendor PCM responsibilities, see [Platform/Vendor Contract](../../platform_contract).

# Display Service

The display service coordinates brightness and screen power state. The platform display port performs the actual operations, while the service manages system requests and their effects.

Brightness values range from 0–100. Brightness changes can take effect immediately or use preset transition durations; temporary brightness preserves the previous value for the system to restore. Display power control is used to wake or turn off the screen, and applications should not bypass power management policies to directly operate the platform port.

Display Service synchronously calls device brightness operations and maintains the requested value; the brightness operation in the device table is required, while power on/off is optional and currently has no physical completion callback. The LVGL framebuffer, refresh, and input devices are provided by the platform graphics HAL and are not part of the brightness/power operation table. An application observing brightness state does not equate to device confirmation. See [Application Contract](../../application_contract) and [Platform/Vendor Contract](../../platform_contract).

# Haptic Service

The haptic service maps system feedback requests to the platform vibration device. When the device is missing or an operation is unsupported, the service reports according to device capabilities and operation results; a silent no-effect does not constitute a success confirmation.

The service provides three global strength levels — off, normal, and enhanced — as well as feedback semantics such as short, stronger, and long. The specific waveform and duration are determined by the platform implementation; callers express feedback intent and do not directly control the vibration hardware.

Core synchronously invokes the Vibrator's on/off operations according to feedback intent; the Vendor determines the actual waveform and device strength. The operations have no return value, and the current Service does not provide per-vibration completion or hardware success events, so applications cannot rely on a given request necessarily producing a perceptible vibration. See [Platform/Vendor Contract](../../platform_contract) for the platform boundary.

# Script Engine Overview

The script runtime lets Applications and Watchfaces share a single JavaScript execution, Realm, module loading, and Native API boundary. It is coordinated by three different owners: the App/Watchface Manager selects the installed identity and Activity to open; SPM manages script program instances and their lifecycle; Script Engine Core executes JS; SNI safely connects registered capabilities and Native resources to each program Realm. The App/Watchface Manager requests program startup and resumption through SPM, and SPM is the management boundary between the program lifecycle and Script Engine Core.

## Core State and Program Lifecycle

Script Engine Core is a global JavaScript executor responsible for engine initialization, Realm, module resolution, execution, garbage collection, and engine-level error recovery. SPM creates a Program with an independent Realm and SNI context, and stores the installed identity, type, permissions, and the `ACTIVE`, `SUSPENDED`, `STOPPING`, `TERMINATED` lifecycle states. Core's execution state describes the current engine invocation window and is not equal to the lifecycle of a particular Program: after `main.js` finishes executing, Core can return to `IDLE` while the Program remains `ACTIVE`, and its Realm can still be re-entered through timer/event callbacks.

| Layer | State it owns | State it does not own |
|---|---|---|
| App / Watchface Manager | Installed ID, entry selection, startup/switching flow for the corresponding Activity | JerryScript Realm and SNI Native resources |
| SPM | Program instance, Realm association, program state, program-level errors, and callback gate | Activity page stack policy, device service policy |
| Script Engine Core | Global engine state, JS invocation, Realm execution, module resolution, and engine generation | Application navigation, Recent Apps cards, and hardware capabilities |
| SNI | Per-Program JS/Native API mapping, handles, and callback owner | Activity stack, service cache, and Vendor devices |

When an application is retained by Recent Apps, SPM can keep its Program/Realm `SUSPENDED`; resuming restores the same instance and does not re-execute `main.js`. A new application entry runs `main.js` synchronously through SPM; this call occupies the execution context that initiated the launch, and JS does not run in parallel just because a loading Activity is shown first. Different programs cannot execute JavaScript in parallel; scheduling and suspension policy are decided by SPM/the caller.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Manager[App / Watchface Manager] -->|open / resume / suspend / stop| SPM
    SPM -->|select program and Realm| Core[Singleton Script Engine Core]
    Core -->|mount registered APIs| SNI[SNI]
    SPM -->|owns| Program[Program instance + Realm + SNI context]
    SNI -->|typed Native calls| Framework[Activity / UI / Services]
    Framework -->|callback/result| SNI
    SNI -->|active owner Realm| Core
```

## Package Identity and Module Loading

Applications and watchfaces use the same EPKG v1 `.epk` container; `package_type` distinguishes Application from Watch Face, the `id` in `manifest.json` is the runtime identity, the API level is used for compatibility checks, and permission declarations are used for the authorization flow before launch. Package format, integrity verification, and installation belong to the Package/App boundary; the Script Engine receives an already-prepared program package and is not responsible for transport, installation, or uninstall UI. For the installation package structure, see [EPKG v1 Installation Package Format](./package_format); for the project and build tools, see [ElenixOS-Toolkit](../development/toolkit).

`main.js` is the program entry point. Module resolution is based on the program package path, normalizes module identifiers, and caches resolution results to maintain module instance semantics within the same program; the corresponding module state is cleaned up when the program/engine is released. Scripts can import files through the current package's module resolution mechanism, but this does not mean that a general-purpose Storage API automatically forms an application sandbox; the file access boundary is defined by the corresponding public API, see [Storage Contract](./services/storage).

## API and Native Extension Boundary

Each Realm mounts the registered `lv` and `eos` APIs at creation time. SNI descriptions/bindings determine what scripts can call, how Native values are converted, who owns objects, and which Realm a callback returns to. An arbitrary C function or Vendor driver does not automatically become a script capability just because it is linked into the system; new script capabilities are selected from stable Framework/Service interfaces and explicitly registered through SNI.

Handle allocation, invalidation, explicit deletion, and fallback cleanup on program stop are part of the SNI contract. The types, return semantics, and lifecycle of public APIs constitute the script interface; internal handle numbering, Realm switching methods, resource linked lists, generator artifacts, and Native address mapping are implementation details. For specific ownership, suspension, and asynchronous callback rules, see [SNI Architecture and Lifecycle](./script_engine/sni).

## Exceptions, Engine Rebuild, and Program Recovery

Syntax/module errors, catchable JavaScript exceptions, and JerryScript fatal errors are different failure paths. A normal program stop ends a Program/Realm; a fatal reset rebuilds the JerryScript heap and the SNI global registration state within the current process. It does not restart the operating system process.

### Normal stop and Core Cleanup

When SPM normally terminates a Program, it first closes that program's callback gate, cleans up SNI references and page resources, and then calls Core stop/release Realm. Core releases the current Realm, module references, and execution state and returns to `IDLE`; the JerryScript global heap remains available for subsequent Programs. The full Core clean-up path separately calls `jerry_cleanup` and enters `UNINITIALIZED`, which is not at the same level as the normal stop of each Program.

### Fatal reset capture and rebuild

JerryScript's fatal port returns to the recovery point via `setjmp`/`longjmp` within the fatal scope established by Core. During a Program's first run, the scope is established by `script_engine_run`; when subsequently entering JerryScript from a callback, the scope is established by the callback invocation path. Core saves the identity and error information of the crashed Program, then rebuilds the engine in the following order:

1. Clean up the module queue, module references, Realm switching state, and current script package state held by Core.
2. SPM marks all Programs as `STOPPING`, suspends LVGL timer dispatch, cleans up event descriptors and Sensor requests, invalidates timer/animation callbacks, cleans up Program Views, and destroys all SPM Programs and Recent Apps records.
3. The fatal heap may still contain JerryScript handles that cannot be safely inspected or freed. The recovery path does not perform a normal SNI resource sweep; to avoid using records that are corrupted or still on the C call stack, some SNI/Native bookkeeping and resources are retained. The old SNI context shells and Program records are invalidated.
4. Core calls `jerry_init` to reinitialize the JerryScript heap, calls `sni_init` to rebuild the SNI type and API registration state, increments the engine generation, then reopens LVGL timers and sets the Core state to `IDLE`.
5. New Programs create new Realms, SNI contexts, and wrappers through the regular SPM startup path. Old Realms, JS values, handles, callbacks, and Programs are not restored or migrated.

This recovery only holds within a valid fatal scope. If a JerryScript fatal occurs at a location with no active scope, or is triggered again during fatal recovery itself, the current port aborts the process and cannot transition into the rebuild flow described above.

### How applications are handled after a rebuild

Core automatically rebuilding JerryScript does not mean that every crashed Program is automatically restarted. Program-level recovery is determined by the triggering path and the application type:

| Scenario | Handling after engine rebuild |
| --- | --- |
| Fatal during the first launch of main.js | After `script_engine_run` completes the heap rebuild, it returns the execution error to the launcher; the launcher displays the error and handles the failure, and no separate delayed fatal event is published. |
| Fatal in a runtime callback of an Application | Core publishes `EOS_EVENT_SCRIPT_FATAL` with a delay; the App manager displays a Restart/Exit error panel. After choosing Restart, a new Activity and a new SPM Program restart the application; the default path does not automatically restart that application. |
| Fatal in a runtime callback of a JavaScript Watchface | The Watchface manager displays a Restart/Switch panel; after the user chooses, a new Activity and Program are rebuilt through the regular watchface switching path. |
| Console fatal | The delayed fatal event is handled by the App manager: clean up the old Activity sub-stack and recreate the Watchface; if the foreground before the crash was a script Application, restore that application with a new Activity and a new Program. Native/System Applications are not restarted as script Programs. |

Fatal notifications during callback execution are published with a delay via `Dispatcher`, so that Core completes the heap rebuild and timer recovery before entering the App/Watchface handling path. SNI loses all old contexts in a global reset; for the local boundaries of handle and resource cleanup, see [SNI Architecture and Lifecycle](./script_engine/sni).

Ordinary `SUSPENDED`, engine `IDLE`, or catchable script exceptions are different states from a fatal reset; whether Realms, Activities, and service requirements are retained depends on the lifecycle contract of the corresponding owner.

## Execution Time and Thread Boundary

Script Engine Core does not provide parallel JS threads. `main.js`, ordinary synchronous SNI APIs, and callbacks in `spm_call` all run on the current call stack; a timer, LVGL event, or Native async request only determines when JS is entered again, and does not turn a callback into a background thread. Native callbacks are delivered into the registered owner's Realm by a runtime context suitable for operating on JerryScript.

By default, Core limits a single synchronous JS execution to 3000 ms. JerryScript periodically calls the stop callback during VM execution, and Core checks the elapsed time based on the monotonic tick since startup; a timeout ends the current JS execution and returns to the calling path with `EOS_ERR_TIMEOUT`. Native Core can set the threshold to `0` to disable this check.

The stop callback only checks time while JerryScript is executing, and does not preempt a Native C function that has already been entered and is blocking. If file I/O, decoding, a Native API, or a synchronous callback occupies the current call stack for a long time, it will still delay the UI/Core main loop; whether there is a Dispatcher or a device-specific queue depends on the corresponding service contract. Therefore, execution timeout only covers the JS execution intervals that the VM can check.

## Continue Reading by Lifecycle Topic

- [Application / Framework Contract](./application_contract): installation identity, launch, suspension, resumption, and program stop.
- [Runtime](./runtime): system-level relationships among Activity, View, events, thread contexts, and platform initialization.
- [SNI Architecture and Lifecycle](./script_engine/sni): JS handles, callbacks, asynchronous requests, and teardown ordering.
- [Platform / Vendor Contract](./platform_contract): device and service boundaries beneath the script API.

The log service filters by severity level and dispatches formatted messages to registered listeners. The system provides four levels: debug, info, warning, and error; the global minimum level determines which messages are dispatched.

# Power Management Service

The Power Manager maintains the display/sleep policy as seen by the Core and hands the required power actions to the power device. It is the owner of the system state, not a feedback sensor for the physical power controller; the software state observed by callers does not necessarily prove that the hardware has completed the transition.

## Requests, States, and Platform Actions

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Input as Framework / Input
    participant PM as Power Manager
    participant Event as Event Bus
    participant Sensor as Sensor Service
    participant Device as Power Device / Vendor

    Input->>PM: request sleep / wake
    PM->>PM: update Core software state
    PM->>Event: synchronously publish sleep / AOD / display-on
    Event->>Sensor: recompute sensor power policy
    PM->>Device: set_power(state)
```

The system states are display-on, AOD, and sleep. A sleep request turns into AOD when AOD mode is enabled, otherwise it enters sleep; a wake turns into display-on. State events are published by the synchronous Event Bus, and then the service performs the platform `set_power` operation.

Currently the return value of `set_power` is not propagated to the caller, and the state is not rolled back on platform errors; when the power device is missing, the Core logs an error, but there is no generic asynchronous "hardware rejected/completed" result. The event indicates that the Core state has changed, not that the hardware has confirmed it. If a product requires reliable confirmation, an explicit confirmation and failure contract must be added for the Power Device/Service.

Sleep pauses the Power Manager's timer; the sensor service observes the synchronous state events, applies an interval floor in low-power/AOD mode, turns off sensors during sleep but retains the demand, and restores them according to the remaining demand after wake.

## Upper-Layer and Lower-Layer Responsibilities

- The Framework, input, and system policy request sleep/wake, always-on mode, or a timeout; applications do not directly rewrite the device power state.
- The Power Manager is responsible for the software state, timeout policy, configuration, and state events; it does not own board-level power rails, display panel sequences, or chip sleep flows.
- The Vendor registers the state transition operations of the power device and implements the states that the target platform can support. Successful device registration does not mean that every state such as AOD or sleep has a hardware implementation.
- When the platform cannot provide a certain state, the integration should explicitly express the capability; the current single `set_power(state)` interface has no generic discovery protocol for independently querying the support status of each state.

Automatic sleep only happens when the service actually creates a timer. The timeout setting only updates the period of an existing timer; if the current build/configuration does not create a timer, an explicit request can still change the software state, but it will not be triggered automatically by the timeout.

The current Core source hardcodes `DEBUG_DISABLE_TIMER` to `1`, so the current build does not create an automatic sleep timer. When the configuration key `sleep_timeout_sec` is missing, the period baseline is 15 seconds, but this value only takes effect in target builds that create a timer; in the current Simulator/this Core version, waiting 15 seconds will not automatically enter AOD or sleep. Explicit sleep/wake requests and input wake state transitions still work along the paths described above.

For platform responsibilities, see [Platform/Vendor Contract](../../platform_contract); for the input wake path, see [UI and Input Architecture](../../ui).

# Metric Service

The Metric Service provides stable semantic data names for watch faces and scripts, mapping different sources such as time, battery, and sensors into unified data samples. It separates "what the data is" from "which device the data comes from," so watch face components do not need to depend directly on sensor types or board-level interfaces.

## Data Path```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Time[时间服务] --> Metric[Metric 语义映射]
    Battery[电池服务] --> Metric
    Sensor[传感器服务与算法] --> Metric
    Metric -->|read / subscribe| SNI[SNI: eos.metric]
    Metric -->|绑定的语义值| Widget[eos.ww 组件]
    SNI --> Script[脚本应用或表盘]
```The service returns to consumers the value, unit, sample timestamp, validity, and stale status corresponding to a semantic name. It typically reads data from existing services or derives values from time; it does not copy underlying sensor caches, nor is it responsible for device drivers, raw sampling, or historical databases.

## Current Metric Names and Units

| Name | Value and Unit | Validity Rule on First Read |
|---|---|---|
|`time.now`| Seconds elapsed in the current day, in`s`; does not include the date. | The current implementation always marks it`valid=true`. When the time device is not registered, the time service returns a zero value, so the Metric displays`0 s`and is still a valid sample. |
|`battery.percent`| Battery percentage, in`%`, valid range 0–100. | Valid after a valid Battery report is received; otherwise`valid=false`. |
|`battery.charging`| Charging state, in`bool`;`value`is 0 or 1. | The current implementation returns`valid=true`and`false`even when Battery has no valid report yet; when you need to determine whether battery data is available, also check`battery.percent.valid`. |
|`health.heart_rate`| Heart rate, in`bpm`. | Requires a non-zero timestamp and a non-zero heart rate sample; marked`stale=true`after 30 seconds. |
|`health.spo2`| Blood oxygen saturation, in`%`, typically 0–100. | Requires a non-zero timestamp and a non-zero SpO₂ sample; marked stale after 30 seconds. |
|`activity.steps`| Monotonically accumulated step count, in`steps`. | Requires a sensor sample timestamp; marked stale after 10 seconds. |
|`environment.temperature`| Temperature, in`degC`. | Derived by dividing the raw milli-°C by 1000; marked stale after 10 seconds. |
|`environment.pressure`| Absolute barometric pressure, in`Pa`. | Directly uses the Pa field from BARO; marked stale after 10 seconds. |
|`orientation.heading`| Azimuth, in`deg`, range`[0, 360)`, increasing clockwise. | Comes from the compass algorithm; marked stale after 10 seconds. Subscribing to this Metric acquires the compass sensor requirement. |
|`moon.phase`| Lunar phase cycle ratio, in`phase`, with one synodic month normalized to`[0, 1)`. | Calculated from the platform's current date; valid and not stale. |
|`moon.illumination`| Estimated illumination ratio, in`%`, range 0–100. | Calculated from the platform's current date; valid and not stale. |

The Metric's`timestamp`for sensor sources is the monotonic millisecond timestamp since boot of the collected sample; for time, battery, and date-derived values, it is the monotonic millisecond timestamp since boot at the time of reading. It is not the unit of the value itself described by the`unit`field.

Scripts can read a Metric once synchronously or establish a periodic subscription. The subscription callback is bound to the SNI program context that created it and executes when that context is runnable; unsubscribing or destroying the context releases the subscription. When the data comes from a sensor, the subscribed value still represents the latest cache of the Sensor Service and does not mean that each callback triggers a hardware sample. Sampling freshness is determined jointly by sensor requirement arbitration, device capabilities, and the Metric's valid/stale flags.

Watch face components can bind directly to known Metrics, or scripts can read Metrics and then control components themselves. Components are responsible for display and their own LVGL resources, while the Metric Service is responsible for the semantics of values and source mapping; neither components nor Metrics depend directly on device operation tables.

## Extension Boundaries

The current Metric names and source mappings are defined by a static set within the service; there is no dynamic Provider registry or priority selection mechanism. When adding a new hardware source, first extend the corresponding device/service contract; only values that need to be expressed stably across applications are added to the Metric semantic mapping. Only afterward does the script boundary or watch face component choose whether to expose and present that value.

Therefore, new consumers or watch face components that use existing Metrics do not need to change the data source; adding a new Metric requires extending the service mapping and the corresponding SNI boundary. The mere existence of an underlying sensor does not mean that a corresponding Metric already exists on the script side, nor does it mean that a general-purpose registerable Provider exists.

## Current Implementation Boundaries

- Common sources are read through time, battery, and the Sensor Service; some semantic values are derived by the service.
- Sensor Metric reads use the service cache and do not replace the raw sensor subscription and sampling requirement APIs.
- Currently only subscriptions to`orientation.heading`acquire the corresponding compass algorithm request; the subscription period of other Metrics itself does not guarantee that underlying hardware sampling is started.
- Currently`battery.charging`still returns`false`and`valid=true`when there is no valid Battery Service report; when determining whether battery data is available, JS also checks`battery.percent.valid`. This behavior is specific semantics of this Metric and does not apply to all boolean Metrics.
- Metric is a semantic adaptation layer for display and scripts, not a general-purpose data warehouse for all system data.

For related boundaries, see [Application Contract](../../application_contract), [Sensor Service](../sensor), [SNI Architecture and Lifecycle](../../script_engine/sni), and [Watch Face System](../../framework/watchface).

# State Service

The state service stores system state that must persist across runtime instances, and is distinct from the configuration service: configuration describes adjustable settings, while state records data formed during operation, such as battery capacity information.

The service stores boolean, string, and numeric types by key, and writes state to the system state file. When reading a missing value, the caller provides a fallback value; dynamic strings and parsed JSON data are freed by the receiver according to its resource rules.

The persistence path is managed by the system storage configuration. Application scripts use isolated application configuration; the system state file is not part of the application script's configuration boundary.

The state service owns system persistent state keys and values; consumers pull the current value and handle defaults, and do not write the state file directly. Persistence capability depends on the Storage/platform filesystem port; state is not an event log or an application-private configuration space. See [Application Contract](../../application_contract) and [Storage Service](../storage).

# Time Service

The time service provides the system and applications with a unified view of date and time. The platform time port is responsible for reading the current time, and the service converts it into a common date-time representation and reports initialization or read errors.

Consumers should obtain the system time through the time service, and should not access the platform clock themselves or assume that all platforms have the same time zone and time synchronization source.

Time reading is a synchronous pull: the Core calls the registered time device and obtains a value returned in the common date-time type; when the time device does not exist, the caller cannot assume that a valid time is available. The Platform is responsible for the clock source, RTC/time synchronization, and conversion, and the Core does not provide an asynchronous time update stream. For the responsibilities of the upper and lower layers, see the [Application Contract](../../application_contract) and the [Platform/Vendor Contract](../../platform_contract).

# Sensor Service

Sensor Service is the state and sampling coordinator between sensor devices and Native consumers. Devices provide sampling control and standard samples; the service holds per-type FIFO/latest, Native subscriptions, and sampling demands; applications obtain data by reading, subscribing, or through higher-level Metrics. JS currently does not directly subscribe to raw Sensor samples.

## Protocol from Request to Sample

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Consumer as Native Consumer
    participant Service as Sensor Service
    participant Device as Sensor Device
    participant Vendor as Platform / Sensor Driver

    Consumer->>Service: read / subscribe / get sampling demand
    Service->>Service: merge consumer demands of the same type
    Service->>Device: enable / disable / set sample rate
    Device->>Vendor: invoke registered device operations
    Vendor-->>Service: notify standard sample
    Service->>Service: rate filter, copy and update FIFO/latest
    Service-->>Consumer: synchronous subscription callback
    Consumer->>Service: unsubscribe / release own demand
    Service->>Device: recompute based on remaining demands
```

Vendor's control and data directions are opposite: the service issues enable/rate to the device based on effective demands; Vendor hands back the standard type, data, and acquisition time to the service after obtaining a sample. `eos_sensor_notify` copies the input parameters, maintains the FIFO and latest, and synchronously iterates subscribers outside the critical section. The sample pointer received by the callback is only valid during that callback; it must be copied to be retained.

## How Consumers Read or Subscribe

- Native Pull can take the earliest unconsumed sample from the FIFO, or read a latest snapshot that does not consume the FIFO. Returns not-found/invalid when there is no sample yet; a zero value can be a valid sample, and only the timestamp and validity indicate whether data has ever been received.
- Native Push subscriptions are held by the service. When the subscription's minimum interval is greater than zero, an independent sampling demand is also created; when the interval is zero, only the callback is registered and it is not responsible for starting the sensor. Unsubscribing releases that subscription's own demand, and self-unsubscription within a callback is deferred to a broadcast safe point for cleanup.
- Algorithm requests and explicit demands each also have their own demand ID. The compatibility interface `eos_sensor_set_sample_period` is not a per-consumer isolated handle: the current implementation has only one shared compatibility demand per type, and multiple callers update the same demand. New Native consumers should use an independent demand lifecycle.
- JS `eos.sensor.readLatest` reads the service cache but has no raw subscribe. `eos.metric` can periodically notify semantic data; for sensor sources, it reads the Sensor Service cache and does not guarantee that one callback corresponds to one hardware sample.

## Arbitration, State, and Effective Period

The service takes the shortest interval among all effective demands per type, then applies the current power policy's minimum interval or disable policy. The sampling period is the output cadence required by consumers, not the hardware ODR that Vendor must precisely achieve; whether the device can accept it is reflected through operation capabilities and state. Releasing one consumer must not lower/disable a sensor still needed by other consumers.

Switching from display-on to AOD uses the low-power lower bound; sleep turns off active devices but retains demands, and on wake recomputes based on still-effective demands. Establishing a demand may fail when the service lacks a bound device, the device state is error, or the current policy prohibits enabling; Core should not fabricate valid samples.

### Sample Fields, Units, and Capacity

Native `eos_sensor_data_t` and JS `eos.sensor.readLatest()` use the following standard semantics. Only fields already exported by SNI can be read from JS; among them, `timestamp` exists for all JS results.

| Type | Field | Unit and Conversion |
|---|---|---|
| `ACCE` | `x/y/z` | milli-m/s²; divide by 1000 to get m/s², approximately 9807 represents 1 g. |
| `GYRO` | `x/y/z` | milli-deg/s; divide by 1000 to get deg/s. |
| `MAG` | `x/y/z` | nT; divide by 1000 to get µT. |
| `TEMP` | `temp` | milli-°C; divide by 1000 to get °C. |
| `BARO` | `pressure`, `temperature` | pressure is absolute Pa; temperature is milli-°C, divide by 1000 to get °C. |
| `HUMIDITY` | `humidity` | milli-%RH; for example 50000 represents 50.000 %RH. |
| `LIGHT` | `lux` | lux, no scaling. |
| `PROXIMITY` | `distance_mm` | mm, no scaling. |
| `HR` | `heart_rate` | BPM, no scaling. |
| `SPO2` | `spo2` | percentage, typically 0–100. |
| `STEP` | `steps` | monotonically accumulated step count, not step rate or delta. |
| `ECG` / `CAP` | `ecg` / `cap` | project-defined source counts; there is currently no dependable physical calibration for voltage or capacitance. |
| `PPG` | `red` / `ir` | optical front-end ADC counts; this is the raw optical source value, not a heart rate result. |

The sample timestamp is the platform's monotonic milliseconds since boot at acquisition time, not wall-clock or Unix time. A value of zero can be valid data; when there is no sample yet, the Native latest API returns `EOS_ERR_NOT_FOUND`, while JS's initialized valid types can still return all-zero fields, so JS callers should check `timestamp` and not merely whether the object is `null`.

Three-axis data uses the ElenixOS right-handed device coordinate system. The Core contract fixes the right-handedness of the coordinates, while the physical mounting orientation is specified by each board-level platform; the platform completes chip axis and mounting transformations before reporting, and applications no longer perform axis swaps/flips per board or chip.

Each Sensor Type's FIFO holds 64 samples by default. When there is insufficient write space, the oldest entry is discarded to accept the newest sample; the latest snapshot is updated independently and is not affected by FIFO consumption. The sampling period is an output cadence request and does not guarantee a precise hardware ODR.

## Lifecycle and Context

The Sensor device must be registered before the Sensor Service; the Service fixes the current default device for each type and creates caches during initialization. Registration later than service initialization will not automatically rebind, and there is currently no sensor hot-plug, default device priority, or failover mechanism. Platform integration must also separately initialize the Sensor Service; `eos_init()` currently does not handle this step.

Native subscriber nodes and demands are managed by the consumer owner. Native Activity or program termination does not automatically invalidate arbitrary `user_data` and replace unsubscription; the owner must explicitly unsubscribe in the stop/destroy path. SNI-managed Metric callbacks, however, belong to the script context, are checked by SNI per program/generation, and are released when the context is cleaned up.

`eos_sensor_notify` synchronously executes Native consumer callbacks in the publisher's context. Therefore, if Vendor obtains data from an ISR, it must first defer through a platform task/Dispatcher to a context where Core callbacks are allowed to execute; unless it can be proven that the entire downstream callback chain is ISR-safe. The service does not call consumers while holding a critical section, but it also does not automatically redirect publishing to the LVGL main loop.

## Handoff Boundaries

- [Platform/Vendor Contract](../../platform_contract): registration timing, sample conversion, notify context, and multi-device selection rules.
- [Application Contract](../../application_contract): consumption rules for Pull, Native subscription, Metric, and program lifecycle.
- [Metric Service](../metric): the semantic data boundary for watch faces/scripts.
