# File System Module

The storage service provides synchronous JSON, file, and directory operations on top of a platform file-system port. Currently, whole-file writes perform file operations directly, with no active batched deferred-write queue. The platform port is responsible for the file-system implementation of the current target; the service API accepts paths and handles and does not imply an application identity or script sandbox.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Consumer[Framework / App] -->|sync path operation| Storage[Storage Service]
    Storage -->|FS operation| Port[File-system Port]
    Port -->|data / error| Storage
    Storage -->|result / owned value| Consumer
```

## JSON and File Data

JSON data supports typed reads and updates. When a key is missing or the type does not match, reads use the caller-provided fallback value. Dynamic strings and parsed JSON trees are freed by the caller according to their allocation source.

JSON and whole-file data writes complete within the current call; recursive deletion affects the entire target directory tree, and the path boundary must be confirmed before calling.

## File and Directory Resources

Files and directories are accessed through explicit handles. A failed open returns an invalid handle; a handle becomes immediately unusable once closed, and subsequent reads and writes are no longer valid. Directory reads write entries one by one into a caller-provided buffer. Space queries and other device capabilities may be unsupported depending on the platform, and callers identify failures through the return result.

File handles and whole-file convenience APIs both access the file system on the current call path; large-file I/O may occupy the calling context. The write of the whole-file API returns the result of the current write operation, but does not indicate that a higher-level application transaction has been atomically committed.

## LVGL File System Adaptation

When the Storage Service initializes, it registers an LVGL file-system driver adapter. LVGL's open, read, write, seek, and directory operations are routed through this adapter to the same storage service handle interface; the read cache is disabled, and when a file/directory is closed the adapter closes the corresponding Storage handle and frees its wrapper record. The driver letter is determined by the build configuration and is kept consistent with LVGL's default file-system drive letter.

## Paths and Isolation

The script interface constructs the package `assets/` and application/watch-face configuration directories based on the current program identity; these path rules belong to the SNI layer. The generic Storage API does not rewrite or restrict paths based on the current script identity, and therefore does not provide an automatically isolated application sandbox. Newly added JS file capabilities define path constraints at their interface boundary before calling the generic storage operations.

The system uses logical paths beginning with `/`. `EOS_SYS_ROOT_DIR` determines the mapping from the logical root to the platform file system: Simulator Native sets it to the repository's `fs/` directory, WASM uses the `/` virtual root, and MCU platforms typically use the root directory `/` of a mounted file system. As a result, application package and system directory names are consistent across platforms, but their actual absolute paths on the host differ.

| Logical Path | Content |
|---|---|
| `/.sys/config/cfg.json` | System configuration file. |
| `/.sys/app/apps/<app-id>/` | Installed Application; the root directory contains `manifest.json` and the runtime entry `main.js`. |
| `/.sys/app/app_data/<app-id>/` | Application persistent data directory, e.g. the application configuration used by `eos.config`. |
| `/.sys/wf/faces/<watchface-id>/` | Installed Watch Face; the root directory contains `manifest.json` and the runtime entry `main.js`. |
| `/.sys/wf/wf_data/<watchface-id>/` | Watch Face persistent data directory. |
| `/.sys/res/font/` | System font resources; the default TTF relative filename is `font.ttf`. |

Under Simulator Native, for example, `/.sys/app/apps/demo/main.js` corresponds to `fs/.sys/app/apps/demo/main.js` in the repository. In many places, Core uses a fixed buffer of `EOS_FS_PATH_MAX` bytes when composing paths; the Simulator project defaults to 256 bytes, and the buffer must also leave room for the trailing NUL. This is not a rejection rule unified across APIs: the return value or truncation handling for overlong paths is determined by the specific API. The buffer size can be adjusted via the File system configuration group in Kconfig. For platform mapping and build defaults, see [Kernel Configuration System](../../../development/kconfig).

The platform port is responsible for mapping logical paths to the target file system and for providing the results of operations such as open/read/write/seek; it does not determine whether a given script is authorized to access that path. Script resource encapsulation, application configuration namespaces, and any path normalization/out-of-bounds rejection logic must be handled by the upper-layer API that calls it.

For application paths and caller responsibilities, see [Application Contract](../../application_contract); file-system registration and the virtual root are defined by the [Platform/Vendor Contract](../../platform_contract).

# Panel

Panel is a universal content panel that can be placed on an Activity View or any LVGL parent object. It can display an icon, title, message, extra content slot, and confirm/cancel buttons.

## Creation

```c
eos_panel_t *panel = eos_panel_create(parent, &cfg);
eos_panel_t *overlay = eos_panel_create_on_activity(activity, &cfg);
```

`eos_panel_create_on_activity` creates a foreground panel on the Activity's existing View and hides the Activity's application header; after the panel is deleted, the original View remains underneath. The regular `eos_panel_create` only uses the parent object provided by the caller.

## Configuration

```c
eos_panel_cfg_t cfg = {
    .icon_type = EOS_PANEL_ICON_TYPE_SYMBOL,
    .icon_src = LV_SYMBOL_WARNING,
    .title_text = "Warning",
    .message_text = "Are you sure you want to continue?",
    .confirm_btn_text = "OK",
    .confirm_cb = on_confirm,
    .cancel_btn_text = "Cancel",
};
```

The title and message can use text or language string IDs. When a button ID is 0, the corresponding button is hidden; when the confirm callback is empty, no action is taken by default, and when the cancel callback is empty, `eos_activity_back()` is executed by default.

## Extra Content and Release

```c
lv_obj_t *slot = eos_panel_get_extra_slot(panel);
eos_panel_delete(panel);
```

Extra content is added to the returned slot. When the panel container is deleted, the component automatically releases its management structures; the caller may also explicitly call `eos_panel_delete`. After the panel is deleted, the handle becomes invalid, and repeated deletion is not a valid operation.

# UI Components Module

ElenixOS UI is built on LVGL, but UI ownership and hierarchy are jointly constrained by Activity, the top-layer registry, and the system UI manager. Components are not an arbitrary collection of LVGL objects.

## UI Model

Activity owns the application page View; system-level components use semantic top-layer slots. A slot corresponds to a permanent container and expresses the hierarchical relationship of application content, page snapshots, application headers, global interaction, system UI, modal UI, secure UI, and debug UI. Slot numbers are ordering semantics, not LVGL child indices, and cannot be persisted.

The message list, control center, and other sibling overlays share the interaction slot. Foreground objects and touch objects within a slot are reordered through a unified focus mechanism, avoiding each component separately seizing the top layer. Modal, lock screen, error, and permission UI reside at specified higher layers.

## Responsibilities

- Activity manages page Views, page transitions, and page destruction.
- The Overlay layer manages system-level containers and stable visual hierarchy.
- The Interaction slot manages the current focus and input objects of sibling interactive overlays.
- Components are responsible for their own internal objects and callbacks, but not for deleting shared slots, Activity Views, or the root objects of other components.
- Scripts create objects through the registered `lv`/`eos` APIs; script handles remain bound by the owning View and program lifecycle.

## Input and Rendering Flow

Input devices do not share a single event queue that can make decisions on behalf of all inputs. Platform touch is handed to the touch input layer via the LVGL pointer indev, and then hit-testing and widget event dispatch are performed by the LVGL object tree. The crown knob is bound to the currently scrollable object; the crown button and side button are first converted into system actions, then dispatched by the main loop to Chrome or power management. The foreground relationship of pages and overlays is managed by Activity/Chrome, not inferred by drivers.

Therefore platform ports should report standardized touch, knob, or button states; page navigation, wake-up, opening the control center, and widget interaction are still handled by the system layer. UI callbacks execute in the LVGL/runtime main loop; rendering output is carried by the platform display port.

## Message List and Notification Boundary

The message list is a UI component placed in the shared interaction slot, responsible for displaying list items and details. The current implementation has no general notification broker, notification persistence service, or JS-facing notification delivery API. The `notification` permission category and its settings entry do not by themselves constitute a notification sending/storage contract; this list UI should not be regarded as the owner of a notification service.

## Architecture Constraints

- System components must use semantic top-layer slots and must not rely on the current child index or privately reorder the shared top layer.
- Sibling overlays must obtain focus through the interaction slot; system modal layers, lock screen, and error layers must not be covered by ordinary application overlays.
- Cascading invalidation caused by parent object deletion must be treated by components and script handles as a normal lifecycle outcome.
- Objects managed by Activity/Recent Apps/system overlays can only be released by the corresponding owner; components must not delete root objects across owners.
- UI and SNI callbacks must return quickly and must not block or directly operate LVGL from non-UI threads.

# Simulator Build Tools and Logging

This page describes the CMake / Makefile, Kconfig, and Native logging entry points in the ElenixOS-Simulator repository. These are host-side tools for the desktop Simulator, not a unified build interface for each Board's firmware. Application / Watch Face projects, EPKG builds, and analysis are handled by [ElenixOS-Toolkit](./toolkit); board-level firmware is built according to [Platform and Board Integration](../integration/overview) and the documentation of the corresponding project.

## Build and Configuration

```bash
cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build --parallel
cmake --build build --target menuconfig
```

`menuconfig` uses `kconfiglib` to generate the `.config` and generated configuration header in the build directory. For the configuration override order and available options, see [Kernel Configuration System](./kconfig).

## Application / Watchface Development

Project initialization, EPKG package building, and analysis of existing packages are provided by the official VS Code extension [ElenixOS-Toolkit](./toolkit). The package format itself is defined by [EPKG v1 Package Format](../architecture/package_format).

The `ElenixOS/scripts/eos_pkg_builder.py` in the simulator repository is the legacy standalone packaging tool, currently in a deprecated / legacy state, and is no longer the recommended build entry point for new Application or Watchface projects.

## Running and Logging

The Native build artifact is `bin/main` in the repository root; runtime logs are written to `tmp/latest.log` and archived by time. The WASM build artifact is in the build directory's `bin/`, and requires an HTTP server to serve it to the browser.

The repository does not have the generic `build.sh`, `clean.sh`, `eos_log_i`, and other tool interfaces referred to as legacy in the documentation; for logging, use `EOS_LOG_D/I/W/E` or the script-side `eos.console.*`.

# Testing Overview

The current test application is built on top of the LVGL runtime, providing interactive test pages and a synchronous test framework. It is not a standalone headless command-line test program.

## Test Framework

Tests are registered by name and function into a fixed-capacity test table. The runner can execute all or a subset of tests based on selection, and displays results in the GUI page and logs. Duplicate names do not create a second test; tests exceeding the compile-time capacity are not added.

Test functions execute synchronously within the current call, using the framework-provided recording/assertion interfaces to write results. After a test returns, the runner proceeds to the next selected test; the current implementation has no general asynchronous protocol for suspending a test across multiple LVGL ticks before settling.

## GUI Page

The test application provides a test list, group selection, run progress, and result display. Features that require continuous observation or manual operation (such as UI, sensors, and audio) should use separate interactive pages; the results of such pages are not automatically counted in the synchronous test framework's statistics.

## Compile-Time Switch

The test application is controlled by `EOS_ENABLE_TEST_APP`. When this configuration is disabled, test application-related code is not included in the build. When enabled, tests still require full LVGL/system runtime initialization.

## Current Limitations

- There is no standalone headless runner; a set of tests cannot be run in a pure console environment using only the test framework API.
- Test functions must complete verification before returning; they cannot rely on asynchronous callbacks to change already-recorded results.
- Tests and groups use fixed capacity, with specific limits determined by the current test framework's compile configuration.
- Test registration should be completed before test pages are created, otherwise new entries will not appear in an already-built list.

# Kernel Configuration System

ElenixOS manages compile-time kernel configuration via Kconfig. Final effective values are determined by two independent merge stages: the Kconfig merge layer and the C preprocessor layer.

## Kconfig Merge Layer

The script `kconfig.py genconfig` merges the following three layers using `replace=True` — **later values overwrite earlier ones**:

1. Kconfig built-in `default` statements — kernel-defined baseline defaults
2. Project `defaults.conf` — establishes the baseline for the current platform/product; the Simulator's file is located at `main/src/config/defaults.conf`
3. Build directory `.config` — local `menuconfig` modifications stored in the build directory, with the highest priority

The merge output is written to `build/generated/eos_config_gen.h`. Each value maps one-to-one to its native macro name, emitted under an `#ifndef` guard.

## C Preprocessor Layer

The header `eos_config.h` includes configuration definitions in a fixed order, with all symbols guarded by `#ifndef` — **first definition wins**:

1. Compiler `-D` flags
2. `eos_platform_config.h` — manual platform overrides (optional)
3. `eos_config_gen.h` — Kconfig merge output (optional, auto-generated by the build)
4. `eos_config_defaults.h` — kernel fallback defaults

Any stage can prevent subsequent stages from taking effect, forming a complete override chain from the build command line down to the kernel fallback. For example, the Simulator's Native CMake configuration sets the `EOS_SYS_ROOT_DIR` compile macro to the repository's `fs/` directory, taking precedence over the `/` default in Kconfig.

## Common Simulator Defaults

The table below lists the defaults currently used by the Simulator project's `main/src/config/defaults.conf` that affect day-to-day development or operation. They represent the Simulator baseline when not overridden by the local build directory's `.config`; other BSPs may have different project defaults.

| Kconfig Item | Simulator Default | Impact and Adjustment Entry Point |
|---|---:|---|
| `EOSCFG_COMPILE_MODE_DEBUG` | Enabled | Core runs in Debug compile mode; can be switched to Release in `menuconfig` under Build & Compilation. |
| `EOSCFG_MEM_STDLIB` / `EOS_OVERRIDE_LVGL_STDLIB_MALLOC_ENABLE` | Enabled / Disabled | Core uses the C standard allocator by default; the Simulator does not replace LVGL's stdlib allocator with the EOS allocator by default. Can be switched in the Memory menu. |
| `EOS_MEM_TRACK_ENABLE` / `EOS_MEM_TRACK_TABLE_SIZE` | Configured as Enabled / 4096 entries | These two symbols currently have no Core source consumers, so modifying them will not enable/disable or limit the current allocation tracking; `eos_mem.c` currently records allocation statistics independently. |
| `EOS_CACHE_ENABLE` / `EOS_CACHE_SIZE` / `EOS_CACHE_HEADER_COUNT` / `EOS_CACHE_USE_DEDICATED_MEM` | Enabled / 524288 bytes / 16 entries / Disabled | The LVGL image decode cache budget is 512 KiB, with up to 16 cache header records; the Simulator does not use a dedicated cache memory pool. The budget and count can be adjusted in the Image cache menu. The kernel Kconfig original budget is 393216 bytes, and the Simulator project overrides it to 524288 bytes by default. |
| `EOSCFG_FONT_TTF` / `EOSCFG_FONT_TTF_FILE` | Enabled / Enabled | Loads TrueType fonts from the filesystem by default; `EOS_FONT_TTF_FILE_PATH` is `font.ttf`, relative to the system font resource directory. Large/medium/small fonts default to 30/26/22 px. The font source, path, and size can be changed in the Font menu. |
| `EOS_DISPLAY_WIDTH` / `EOS_DISPLAY_HEIGHT` / `EOS_DISPLAY_RADIUS` | 390 / 450 / 80 px | Default simulated screen geometry; window scaling does not rewrite system display coordinates. Target panel parameters can be set in the Display menu. The brightness configuration range defaults to 5–100. |
| `EOSCFG_FS_POSIX` / `EOS_FS_PATH_MAX` / `EOS_LVGL_FS_LETTER` | POSIX / 256 bytes / `Z` | Default filesystem interface, path buffer limit, and LVGL file drive letter. The configured value `90` corresponds to drive letter `Z`, which must match LVGL's `LV_FS_DEFAULT_DRIVE_LETTER`. Can be adjusted in the File system menu. |
| `EOSCFG_LANG_EN` | Enabled | The Simulator's default UI language on first launch is English; can be changed to Simplified Chinese in the Language menu. |
| `EOS_USE_ASSERT` / `EOS_LOG_ENABLE_STD` / `EOS_LOG_MAX_LISTENERS` / `EOS_LOG_USE_COLOR` | Enabled / Enabled / 8 / Disabled | Assertions and the stdout log listener are enabled by default, with up to 8 log listeners registered; the minimum log level is managed by the runtime logging service, with an initial value of `DEBUG`. Registration returns `-1` when the listener table is full. The Logging menu controls assertions, the stdout listener, capacity, and color output. |
| `EOS_RECENT_APPS_ENABLE` / `EOS_RECENT_APPS_MAX` / `EOS_RECENT_APPS_MEM_HIGH_WATERMARK` | Enabled / 3 / 2621440 bytes | Retains up to 3 suspended apps, with an estimated memory high watermark of 2.5 MiB; evicts by LRU once the limit is reached. Timer recovery re-issues one missed callback by default, and animations resume from the pause point. Can be adjusted in the Recent Apps menu. |
| `EOS_ENABLE_TEST_APP` | Enabled | Includes the built-in test app in the Simulator; can be disabled in the Miscellaneous menu. |

The `.config` in the local build directory overrides the Simulator defaults in the table. To confirm the final configuration of a specific build, check the `.config` and `generated/eos_config_gen.h` in that directory; CMake `-D` arguments and platform configuration macros may also override the generated values during the preprocessing stage.

## Operations

The project root `Makefile` provides the following targets:

| Target | Action |
|--------|--------|
| `make` / `make build` | Build the already-configured `build/` directory |
| `make menuconfig` | Edit `build/.config` and refresh that build directory's `generated/eos_config_gen.h` (`cmake -B build && cmake --build build --target menuconfig`) |
| `make run` | Build and run |

### Dependency Installation

```bash
pip install kconfiglib
```

### Multiple Build Directories

`.config` files are fully isolated per build directory. Native and WASM builds can hold independent configurations:

```bash
# Native
cmake -B build
make menuconfig        # Edit build/.config

# WASM
cmake -B build-wasm -D EOS_PLATFORM=WASM
cmake --build build-wasm --target menuconfig    # Edit build-wasm/.config
```

:::note
`menuconfig` requires terminal curses support. On Windows, use MSYS2 terminal.
:::

## Boundary with CMake Options

CMake options (such as `EOS_PLATFORM`, `USE_FREERTOS`, and optional LVGL backends) control the platform, dependencies, compilation units, and linking behavior. Kconfig manages compile-time configuration macros such as memory strategy, filesystem type, fonts, logging, and Recent Apps. The two have different entry points, but CMake `-D` compile definitions may take precedence over Kconfig macros of the same name; the Simulator's `EOS_SYS_ROOT_DIR` is a real example. Running `menuconfig` saves `.config` and updates the generated header of the configured build directory; after directly editing `.config`, re-run `cmake -B build`.

## CI Behavior

GitHub Actions executes `pip install -r requirements.txt` before the build step. CMake configuration auto-completes Kconfig merge and header generation. Should `genconfig` fail, the build proceeds, falling back to `eos_config_defaults.h`.

## Fallback Mechanism

When Kconfig is not installed or `genconfig` fails, the kernel falls back to `eos_config_defaults.h`. The minimal flow `cmake -B build && cmake --build build` remains available under all conditions.

# Contribution Guide

This guide will help you understand the contribution process, coding standards, and contribution methods for ElenixOS, providing complete guidance for participating in ElenixOS development.

## Coding Standards

### C Language Coding Standards

#### Naming Conventions

- **File names**: Use lowercase letters and underscores, e.g., `eos_app.c`
- **Function names**: Use lowercase letters and underscores, e.g., `eos_app_install`
- **Variable names**: Use lowercase letters and underscores, e.g., `app_id`
- **Constants and macros**: Use uppercase letters and underscores, e.g., `EOS_APP_DIR`
- **Type names**: Use lowercase letters and underscores, e.g., `script_pkg_t`
- **Static variable names**: Use leading underscore + lowercase letters and underscores, e.g., `static int _app_count = 0;`

#### Code Style

The project uses **clang-format v20** for C/C++ code formatting, with the configuration file `.clang-format` in the project root. Key rules include:

- **Indentation**: 4 spaces, no tabs
- **Column limit**: **120** characters per line maximum
- **Brace style**: Allman style (braces on separate lines)
- **Pointer/Reference alignment**: Right-aligned, e.g., `int *p`, `int &r`
- **Condition/Loop statements**: Space between keyword and opening parenthesis, e.g., `if (x)`, `while (x)`
- **Function declarations/definitions**: Return type on the same line as function name
- **Binary operators**: Break before non-assignment operators
- **Consecutive macros/assignments/declarations**: No alignment
- **Blank lines at block start**: Not allowed
- **Maximum consecutive blank lines**: 1
- **Comments**: Doxygen-style comments

For detailed rules, see the `.clang-format` file in the project root.

#### Example

```c
/**
 * @brief Install application
 * @param pkg_path EPK installation package path
 * @return eos_result_t Installation result
 */
eos_result_t eos_app_install(const char *pkg_path)
{
    // Function implementation
    return EOS_OK;
}
```

### JavaScript Coding Standards

#### Naming Conventions

- **Variable names**: Use camel case, e.g., `appId`
- **Function names**: Use camel case, e.g., `installApp`
- **Constant names**: Use uppercase letters and underscores, e.g., `MAX_APP_COUNT`
- **Object properties**: Use camel case, e.g., `appName`

#### Code Style

- **Indentation**: Use 2 spaces for indentation
- **Brackets**: Left and right brackets on separate lines
- **Line length**: Each line of code should not exceed 80 characters
- **Comments**: Use JSDoc-style comments

#### Example

```javascript
/**
 * Install application
 * @param {string} pkgPath - EPK package path
 * @returns {number} Installation result
 */
function installApp(pkgPath)
{
    // Function implementation
    return 0;
}
```

## Code Quality Checks

ElenixOS provides a unified code quality check framework via `ElenixOS/scripts/check.py` to ensure code meets project standards.

### Check Types

Running a check executes the following four checkers sequentially:

| Checker | Name | Description |
|---------|------|-------------|
| architecture | Architecture Constraint Check | Validates code against architecture rules, e.g., `jerry_call()` can only be called in specific files, `malloc`/`free` restricted to the port layer |
| formatting | Code Formatting Check | Uses clang-format v20 to check C/C++ files against `.clang-format` rules |
| style | Code Style Check | Uses clang-tidy (or custom regex rules) to scan for style issues, such as TODO/FIXME without issue references, forbidden functions (`sprintf`, `gets`, etc.) |
| static_analysis | Static Analysis | Runs clang-tidy deep analysis (`--checks='*'`) and cppcheck for comprehensive static analysis |

### Dependency Installation

#### clang-format / clang-tidy

- **Ubuntu / Debian**:
  ```bash
  sudo apt-get install clang-format-20 clang-tidy-20
  ```
- **macOS**:
  ```bash
  brew install llvm@20
  ```
- **Windows**:
  ```powershell
  # Option 1: Official installer (recommended)
  # Download LLVM-20.x.x-win64.exe from https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/releases/
  # After installation, clang-format.exe is at C:\Program Files\LLVM\bin\

  # Option 2: Chocolatey
  choco install llvm

  # Option 3: Scoop
  scoop install llvm

  # Option 4: winget
  winget install LLVM.LLVM
  ```
  Verify with `clang-format --version` in `cmd` or `PowerShell`. Since Windows executables don't have versioned names (`clang-format-20` vs `clang-format`), just use `clang-format` with the `--clang-format` parameter.
- Or build LLVM 20 yourself and ensure `clang-format-20` (Unix) or `clang-format` (Windows) is in your `PATH`

#### Python Dependencies

```bash
pip install pyyaml
```

#### cppcheck (optional, for static analysis)

```bash
sudo apt-get install cppcheck      # Ubuntu/Debian
brew install cppcheck              # macOS
```

### Usage

```bash
# Run all checks (project integrity check)
python3 ElenixOS/scripts/check.py

# Run specific checks (e.g., formatting and architecture only)
python3 ElenixOS/scripts/check.py --check fmt,arch

# Run formatting check only
python3 ElenixOS/scripts/check.py --check fmt

# Auto-fix formatting issues
python3 ElenixOS/scripts/check.py --check fmt --fix

# JSON output (CI mode)

# Writing Tests

When adding new tests to ElenixOS, the first decision is whether the verification requirements should go through the framework layer pipeline or build a standalone GUI page. These two paths serve different verification goals and differ in execution model, result determination, and integration approach. Understanding the applicable scenarios for each and the framework layer's internal workflow is a prerequisite for ensuring test consistency and maintainability.

## Choosing a Test Form

For regression verification of deterministic API results, boundary conditions, and error paths, use the synchronous test framework. When continuous rendering, user interaction, real time passage, or hardware feedback is required, use a standalone GUI page in the test app.

## Synchronous Test Contract

Test functions are called in the LVGL main loop context and must complete verification and record results before returning. Do not block or wait in tests, and do not treat "test has started" as a pass; cross-frame scenarios should be rewritten as conditions that can be checked in a single call, or use a standalone interactive page.

Test result recording follows the framework's current recording rules. After one execution, subsequent asynchronous callbacks cannot reliably overwrite an already-completed test result.

## Naming and Registration

Test names must be unique. The current GUI groups by prefix in the name; keeping tests in the same group using a consistent prefix is sufficient to place them in the same group. Registration should be completed before the test page is created, and added to the runner through the corresponding subsystem's test registration entry.

## Resource Cleanup

Activities, LVGL objects, timers, subscriptions, and files created by tests should be cleaned up when the test ends or the page is destroyed. Activity/View deletion may cascade-delete child objects; tests should not continue using old pointers after deletion. Tests that need to run multiple times should also restore global state to a repeatable initial condition.

## Interactive Pages

For scenarios that cannot be determined in a single synchronous call, such as UI, sensors, and audio, a standalone Activity page can be created, with the page lifecycle managing objects and subscriptions. Standalone pages are responsible for displaying results and are not automatically included in the framework layer's pass/fail aggregation.

## Capacity and Configuration

The test app is controlled by `EOS_ENABLE_TEST_APP`. There are compile-time limits on the number of test entries and groups; when approaching the limit, merge duplicate scenarios or adjust the build configuration rather than assuming the registry will dynamically expand.

# Board-Level Firmware Build Path

Board-level firmware is built by the target Platform / BSP project. ElenixOS Core does not provide a universal firmware command that applies to all SoCs and Boards: the SDK, cross-compiler, configuration, boot image layout, and download method are all determined by the specific board-level project. This page helps Platform / BSP developers choose the corresponding project and follow-up documentation.

## Current Integration Projects

| Target | Status | Next Steps |
|---|---|---|
| PSoC Edge E84 series | In development, no stable port yet. | See [E84 Development Project Build and Flashing](../integration/psoc_edge_e84_build), then follow the project documentation to select the target board and connection method. |
| Custom SoC / Board | Defined by the porting project. | Start with [Platform and Board Integration](../integration/overview) and the [Platform / Vendor Contract](../architecture/platform_contract); once the target project is established, use its build, configuration, and download flow. |

## Distinguish Targets and Artifacts

- **Board-level firmware**: Built by the Platform / BSP project for the target chip and board, then flashed using that project's downloader.
- **Application / Watch Face package**: Built via the application development path as a `.epk`, installed onto a system already running ElenixOS; it is not a firmware image. See [Application Development](./application_development) and [Watch Face Development](./watchface_development) for the project flow.
- **Simulator desktop program**: Built by the standalone Simulator project for desktop iteration; it is not a board-level firmware target. See [Simulator Build and Run](../simulator/build) for commands and how to run it.

Each Platform / Board project should document its own prerequisites, target selection, configuration entry points, build artifacts, and flashing steps. Core compile-time options are managed by Kconfig, while specific project defaults are still determined by the board-level project; see the [Kernel Configuration System](../development/kconfig) for configuration entry points. For Core boundaries and device registration constraints during porting, see the [Platform / Vendor Contract](../architecture/platform_contract); for the relationships between layers within the system, see [System Architecture](../architecture/arch).

# Application Development Tutorial

This tutorial creates a script Application that displays "Hello, ElenixOS!", builds an EPKG installation package, and installs and launches it on the Native Simulator or a board running ElenixOS. An application package is not device firmware; board-level firmware is built and flashed by the target Platform / Board project.

## Prerequisites

- Visual Studio Code 1.136 or later is installed on the host.
- [ElenixOS-Toolkit](../development/toolkit)has been searched for and installed from the VS Code Extensions, or`code --install-extension ElenixOS.elenixos-toolkit`has been executed in a terminal with the`code`command installed.
- There is a target system that has been built and is running: the Native Simulator, or a board that provides ESH, YMODEM receive, and the EPKG Installer. For the Simulator's host dependencies and build steps, see [Environment Preparation](./environment)and [Simulator Build and Run](../simulator/build). For board-level firmware paths, see [Board-Level Firmware Build Paths](./build).

The following paths use`$HOME`and bash/zsh commands. Windows users can use the MSYS2/MinGW shell supported by the project, or complete project and package builds through the VS Code graphical interface.

## 1. Create an Application Project

Create the project parent directory in the host terminal:```bash
mkdir -p "$HOME/ElenixOS-Apps"
```Run **ElenixOS: Open App Tools** in the VS Code command palette, enter the **Create** workspace, and fill in the following information:

| Field | Example Value |
|---|---|
| App name |`Hello ElenixOS`|
| App ID |`com.example.hello`|
| Version |`1.0.0`|
| Author |`Example`|
| Description |`A first ElenixOS application`|
| Project location |`$HOME/ElenixOS-Apps`|

Select **Create App project**. This App ID should not already exist under`$HOME/ElenixOS-Apps/`. The Toolkit will create`$HOME/ElenixOS-Apps/com.example.hello/`, which contains the root-level`manifest.json`and the entry script`main.js`.

## 2. Write the Entry Script

Open`$HOME/ElenixOS-Apps/com.example.hello/main.js`, replace the default entry comment with the page code below, and save:```js
const view = eos.view.active();
const button = new lv.button(view);
button.align(lv.ALIGN_CENTER, 0, 0);

const label = new lv.label(button);
label.setText("Hello, ElenixOS!");
```The`id`in`manifest.json`is the stable identity used during installation and at runtime. The fields generated by the Toolkit can be used directly for this example; for the required fields of EPKG v1 and the semantics of API level, see [Installation Package Format](../architecture/package_format). For the Program, Activity, View, and SNI lifecycles of an Application, see [Application and Framework Contract](../architecture/application_contract).

## 3. Build and Validate the Installation Package

First create the output directory:```bash
mkdir -p "$HOME/ElenixOS-Apps/build"
```In the **Build** workspace of App Package Studio, select **Select App project** and open`$HOME/ElenixOS-Apps/com.example.hello/`. Choose **Application** for Package type and click **Validate project**; after validation passes, click **Build package** and save the output as`$HOME/ElenixOS-Apps/build/hello.epk`. After the build completes, the Toolkit displays the package path; the **Analyze** workspace can be used to view the package identity, type, and file table.

For automated builds, the`etk`CLI can be used. Installing the Marketplace extension is not equivalent to having the`etk`command already available in the host`PATH`; for how to build and install the CLI, see [Toolkit Documentation](../development/toolkit). In a terminal that already has the`etk`command, execute:```bash
etk package build "$HOME/ElenixOS-Apps/com.example.hello" \
  --output "$HOME/ElenixOS-Apps/build/hello.epk" --type app --compression auto
etk validate "$HOME/ElenixOS-Apps/build/hello.epk"
```A complete validation should show EPKG v1, package ID`com.example.hello`, and`Validation: full`.`inspect`is a structural preview and does not replace full payload validation.

## 4. Install and Launch

Choose one deployment path that corresponds to the current running target.

### Run on the Native Simulator

First generate the Native program according to [Simulator Build and Run](../simulator/build). The following commands are executed from the root directory of the`ElenixOS-Simulator`repository:```bash
mkdir -p fs/tmp
cp "$HOME/ElenixOS-Apps/build/hello.epk" fs/tmp/hello.epk
./bin/main
```After the Simulator starts, execute the following one by one at the ESH prompt in the same terminal:```text
pkg validate /tmp/hello.epk
pkg install /tmp/hello.epk
apps
app start com.example.hello
````pkg validate`should return`pkg: valid EPKG v1`, and`apps`should list`com.example.hello`. After launching, the simulated screen displays a centered **Hello, ElenixOS!** button.

### Install on a Running Board

The target firmware needs to register ESH's YMODEM receive,`pkg validate`,`pkg install`, and Application management capabilities. Run **ElenixOS: Open ESH Terminal** in the VS Code command palette and select the device UART. The Toolkit's default serial format is 8N1, with RTS/CTS flow control disabled, and`elenixosToolkit.uartBaudRate`defaults to`921600`; the host rate must match the device side, and this configuration item can be modified in VS Code Settings.

Then run **ElenixOS: Send File or Folder with YMODEM (UART)**, select`$HOME/ElenixOS-Apps/build/hello.epk`, and set the device-side path to`/tmp/hello.epk`. After the transfer completes, execute in the ESH Terminal:```text
pkg validate /tmp/hello.epk
pkg install /tmp/hello.epk
```After complete validation succeeds and installation is done, open **Hello ElenixOS** from the target system's Application list. If the Board uses its own deployment tool or different ESH commands, defer to the corresponding Platform / Board project; the Simulator and the currently in-development E84 integration do not mean that all boards provide the same installation capabilities.

- Script interface reference: [JavaScript API Reference](../architecture/script_engine/elenix_os).
- Package fields, checksums, and type definitions: [EPKG v1 Installation Package Format](../architecture/package_format).

# Simulator Environment Setup

This page only lists the host dependencies for ElenixOS-Simulator; it is not a general toolchain checklist for board-level firmware. Platform / Board projects each require their respective SDK, cross-compiler, and flashing tools. For target selection, see [Board-Level Firmware Build Path](./build).

## Required Tools

The Native Simulator's CMake configuration requires CMake 3.10 or higher, a C compiler supporting C99, a C++ compiler supporting C++17, and the SDL2 development library. The WASM Simulator additionally requires the Emscripten SDK and should be configured with `emcmake` after activating the Emscripten environment. FreeRTOS is already provided with the simulator repository and does not need to be downloaded separately.

The project does not declare fixed minimum CPU, memory, or OpenGL specifications in CMake; actual compilation and runtime capability depends on the host, compiler, and SDL2 environment. The Native configuration adds `-march=native` for the compiler, so the compiler needs to support this option.

## Installation Examples

### macOS

```bash
brew install cmake sdl2 python
```

### Ubuntu / Debian

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install build-essential cmake libsdl2-dev python3 python3-pip
```

On Windows, you can use an MSYS2/MinGW environment that the project can recognize SDL2 in; the documentation does not treat any particular Windows toolchain as a runtime requirement. The key is that CMake, the corresponding compiler, and the SDL2 development files are in searchable paths.

## Verification

```bash
cmake --version
python3 --version
```

If `Could NOT find SDL2` appears during Native configuration, please install the SDL2 development package. When using Kconfig, you can install:

```bash
python3 -m pip install kconfiglib
```

## Get Code

```bash
git clone --recursive https://github.com/ElenixOS/ElenixOS-Simulator.git
cd ElenixOS-Simulator
```

After a non-recursive clone, you can fetch the submodules:

# Simulator Performance Troubleshooting: Memory Integrity Assert

This troubleshooting note applies to LVGL-based Simulator test runs, and is not a general performance conclusion for all ElenixOS Boards. The default configuration and performance of the target platform are determined by its BSP and build configuration.

## Frame rate drops after opening and returning from an app

### Symptoms

When scrolling the app list to test frame rate, the FPS after opening a JS app and returning to the list is noticeably lower than testing directly after system boot. The FPS drop scales with the number of suspended apps (~5-10 FPS per suspended app).

### Cause

`LV_USE_ASSERT_MEM_INTEGRITY` is set to `1` in `lv_conf.h`.

When enabled, LVGL calls `lv_mem_test()` after **every** timer callback (`lv_timer.c`), object-tree operation (`lv_obj_tree.c`), and draw operation (`lv_draw_rect.c`, `lv_draw_label.c`). `lv_mem_test()` walks the entire TLSF memory pool checking every block header. With the built-in TLSF allocator (`LV_STDLIB_BUILTIN`), each suspended app (Recents) adds more allocated blocks. The integrity check slows down linearly with the number of blocks, and the frame rate drops accordingly.

This can be confirmed with macOS Instruments (Time Profiler): samples will show `lv_tlsf_check` / `integrity_walker` / `block_is_free` dominating the frame budget.

### Solution

Set `LV_USE_ASSERT_MEM_INTEGRITY` to `0` in `lv_conf.h`:

```c
#define LV_USE_ASSERT_MEM_INTEGRITY 0
```

This option is useful for catching heap corruption during development, but **must** be disabled when doing any frame-rate, scrolling, or animation performance testing. The other asserts (`LV_USE_ASSERT_NULL`, `LV_USE_ASSERT_MALLOC`) are O(1) checks and safe to leave on.

# ElenixOS-Toolkit

**ElenixOS-Toolkit is a VS Code extension for the ElenixOS development workflow.** It provides project initialization, package building and analysis, simulator debugging, and device serial port functionality through the editor workspace. EPKG is the system-level Package Contract for ElenixOS; the Toolkit Builder and Analyzer generate and read packages according to this contract, and the format semantics are defined by the system contract.```mermaid
flowchart TB
    VSCode["VS Code"] --> Toolkit["ElenixOS-Toolkit extension"]
    subgraph Features["Toolkit capabilities"]
        Studio["App Package Studio"]
        Create["Application project initialization"]
        Build["Package Build"]
        Analyze["Package Analysis / Extract"]
        SimDebug["Native Simulator debug and Webview"]
        Serial["ESH serial terminal and YMODEM transfer"]
        CLI["etk CLI"]
        Core["Shared EPKG Core"]
        Studio --> Create
        Studio --> Build
        Studio --> Analyze
        CLI --> Core
        Build --> Core
        Analyze --> Core
    end
    Toolkit --> Studio
    Toolkit --> SimDebug
    Toolkit --> Serial
    Toolkit --> CLI
```The EPKG Package Contract independently defines the format accepted by the OS, constrains the Builder's output, and guides how the Analyzer and the OS Installer / Loader read the same`.epk`file. Package Build and Package Analysis share the Toolkit's EPKG TypeScript Core. For the formal semantics of the package header, FPMA, manifest, File Table, data region, checksums, and signature reservation, see [EPKG v1 Package Format](../architecture/package_format).

## Obtaining and Installing

- **Extension name:** ElenixOS-Toolkit
- **Editor:** Visual Studio Code; the VS Code Engine requirement declared by the extension is`^1.136.0`.
- **Marketplace identifier:**`ElenixOS.elenixos-toolkit`. Search for this name or identifier in VS Code Extensions and select **Install**; you can also install via the VS Code command line:```bash
  code --install-extension ElenixOS.elenixos-toolkit
  ```- **Marketplace page:** [ElenixOS-Toolkit](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ElenixOS.elenixos-toolkit)- **Source repository:** [ElenixOS/ElenixOS-Toolkit](https://github.com/ElenixOS/ElenixOS-Toolkit)The extension's`publisher`and`name`are`ElenixOS`and`elenixos-toolkit`respectively; the project release workflow publishes a matching version of the VSIX to the Visual Studio Marketplace. The current project has no Open VSX publishing configuration, and the GitHub Releases page has no standalone VSIX download item, so the Marketplace is the configured official installation channel.

### Optional: Installing the`etk`CLI

The Marketplace extension provides the VS Code workspace and does not add the`etk`command to the host shell's`PATH`. To use the CLI in a terminal, script, or CI, the host needs Node.js and npm; build and register the command from the Toolkit repository root:```bash
git clone https://github.com/ElenixOS/ElenixOS-Toolkit.git
cd ElenixOS-Toolkit
npm install
npm run package
npm link
etk --help
````npm run package`generates`dist/cli.js`; the repository's`bin`declares a mapping of`etk`to this file. After success,`etk --help`should list the package build, inspect, validate, extract, and install subcommands. If the shell cannot find the command, confirm that npm's global executable directory is in`PATH`.

## Application and Watch Face Projects

Run **ElenixOS: Open App Tools** in the VS Code command palette to open App Package Studio. The **Create** workspace currently provides Application project initialization: it generates a project directory based on the project name, App ID, version, author, and description, containing`manifest.json`and`main.js`; the initial API level is`0`and can be modified in the project. After creation, you can go directly to the Build workspace.

App Package Studio does not currently provide Watchface project initialization or Watchface templates. It can build an existing Watchface project into a watch face package: in the Build workspace, select the project directory containing a root-level`manifest.json`, and set Package type to **Watch face**. The project must still conform to the runtime's entry point and manifest requirements.

A package project uses the root-level`manifest.json`as the source of identity and metadata. This manifest is subsequently interpreted jointly by the Builder, Analyzer, and system installation flow. For the complete project, build, and deployment tutorial for Applications, see [Application Development](../getting_started/application_development); for manually creating a Watch Face project and installing/running it, see [Watch Face Development](../getting_started/watchface_development). These two tutorials target different development goals.

Simulator debugging uses the VS Code workspace / debug configuration provided by the Simulator repository: when Native debug starts, the extension automatically opens the simulator Webview. When the simulator is not in the current workspace, you can specify the executable path via`elenixosToolkit.simulatorPath`.

## Package Build

The Build workspace of App Package Studio reads the manifest and files from the project directory, displays preview information, performs project validation, and then builds the`.epk`package. The project type can be Application or Watch Face; compression options are`auto`,`none`, and`lz4`. After building, you can go directly to Analyze to view the output package. The Toolkit is responsible for converting the project into the EPKG v1 layout permitted by the contract, without changing the package's identity, metadata, or region definitions.

The Toolkit project also declares a`etk`CLI entry point, using the same Shared EPKG Core, which can be used in terminals, scripts, and automated workflows. In an environment where it has been built and the CLI command has been added to`PATH`, you can use:```bash
etk package build ./my-app --output ./build/my-app.epk --type app --compression auto
etk package build ./my-watchface --output ./build/my-watchface.epk --type watchface
````etk`also provides the`inspect`,`validate`,`extract`, and`install`commands. The CLI build input format follows the same Package Contract as the VS Code Build workspace.

## Package Analysis

The Analyze workspace or`etk inspect`opens an existing EPKG and reads the Header, FPMA, manifest, icon metadata, and File Table. The workspace displays the package type, identity, API range, icons, file paths, entry types, codec, stored / raw lengths, as well as the Header CRC and manifest CRC;`etk inspect --json`also returns the parsed Header / FPMA / File Table fields, including each file entry's CRC and offset. The analyzer reads packages according to the Package Contract; for the format definition, see [EPKG v1 Package Format](../architecture/package_format).

Preview-style inspect reads the structure and quickly previews the content, without decoding ordinary payloads item by item; therefore, a damaged payload may still pass the preview stage.`validate`fully processes`NONE`and`LZ4_BLOCK`file entries, verifying the decoded length and file CRC.`extract`performs full validation before writing out. For the current unsigned EPKG v1, the signature offset / size must be zero; the Toolkit does not yet generate signatures or verify the signature region.```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Project["Project"] -->|Build with Toolkit| Package["EPKG package"]
    Package -->|Analyze with Toolkit| Metadata["Package structure / metadata"]
    Package -->|Install| Installer["OS Installer / Loader"]
```The Builder and Analyzer are symmetric consumers of the contract: the Builder produces valid packages, and the Analyzer parses packages according to the same contract. What the Analyzer displays cannot retroactively narrow the regions already defined in the contract; even if the signature region is already reserved at the format level, it does not thereby become a capability supported by the current analyzer.

## Other ElenixOS Development Workflows

- **Native Simulator and F5 debugging:** The Toolkit works with the ElenixOS Native Simulator, driving the LVGL display in a VS Code Webview with a headless (no local window) simulator process, and forwarding touch and hardware key input. When using the workspace and debug configuration provided by the Simulator repository, pressing F5 automatically connects to the Webview; a normal non-debug session can also run **ElenixOS: Open Simulator**. The current simulator workflow supports macOS, Linux, and Windows.
- **ESH serial terminal:** **ElenixOS: Open ESH Terminal** connects to the device ESH in the VS Code Terminal. On first connection, it selects a port from the serial ports detected by the host; the Toolkit does not set a universal default port path. The default serial format is 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit (8N1), with RTS/CTS hardware flow control disabled.`elenixosToolkit.uartBaudRate`defaults to`921600`, setting only the Toolkit host-side rate; the device-side UART must match.`elenixosToolkit.uartMemoryMode`defaults to`window`, and the selected port and rate are retained until the current VS Code window / extension host ends; after changing to`persistent`, they are saved across restarts and workspaces. All settings can be modified in the **ElenixOS Toolkit** group in VS Code Settings.
- **YMODEM file transfer:** **ElenixOS: Send File or Folder with YMODEM (UART)** can transfer files or directories over the device UART, sharing a single serial session with the ESH terminal. Toolkit YMODEM waits 30 seconds per response by default, with a maximum of 10 retries; during transfer, avoid having other serial tools simultaneously read from or write to that port. After the device receives the data, it can continue processing the package using ESH commands such as`pkg validate`and`pkg install`.
- **Platform serial rate (PSoC-E84 development project):** E84 integration is still in the development stage and has not yet achieved a stable port; the following values correspond to this development project and do not represent an interface commitment for a stable port. The Simulator's virtual ESH does not use a physical serial port. The E84 project's ESH and YMODEM use the BSP`CYBSP_DEBUG_UART`, and the device-side baud rate is`921600`, consistent with the Toolkit default; the receive buffer is 8192 bytes, and`uartstats`in ESH can query the RX overflow count. When connecting to a physical device, the host and device UART rates need to match, and`elenixosToolkit.uartBaudRate`must be set.
- **CLI device installation:**`etk install`transfers a local package to the device via YMODEM, then requests the device to validate, install, and read the package information to confirm the installation result. It uses the device-side Installer and does not bypass the Package Contract.

These features enable the Toolkit to cover the daily workflow from project preparation to package delivery, simulator debugging, and device serial operations. The device results of each workflow are still returned by the ElenixOS side; merely building or previewing does not equal a successful device-side installation.

## Legacy Standalone Packaging Script`eos_pkg_builder.py`is a legacy standalone packaging tool; the current ElenixOS-Toolkit has taken over the new Application and Watch Face project build and package analysis workflows. It is retained only as a historical implementation of the old toolchain. For Application and Watch Face project and Package workflows, start from the corresponding tutorials; the Toolkit is one of the tools used by these two development paths.

# Quick Start

ElenixOS is an open-source embedded operating system for smartwatches and resource-constrained wearable devices. ElenixOS Core provides the Framework, script runtime, system services, and device abstraction; Platform / BSP projects connect these system capabilities to specific SoCs, Boards, and peripherals. Application packages, board-level firmware, and the Simulator desktop program are distinct deliverables.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    App["Application / Watch Face"] -->|Public system interfaces| Core["ElenixOS Core"]
    Core -->|Defines Device / port contracts| Platform["Platform / BSP"]
    Platform -.->|Implements and registers devices| Core
    Platform -->|Integrates| Board["SoC / Board"]
    Board -->|Device data and status| Platform
```

Development tools and the Simulator are auxiliary environments chosen per task, not part of the system runtime.

The currently public PSoC Edge E84 integration is still under development and has not yet formed a stable port. The Simulator is suitable for desktop UI and some platform-independent logic iteration, but does not replace board-level driver, power consumption, timing, and flashing verification.

## Choose Your Development Path

| Goal | Where to Start | What This Path Involves |
|---|---|---|
| **Application Development** | [Application Development Tutorial](./application_development) | Application model, project entry point, EPKG build, installation, and running. The official VS Code project and package workflow use [ElenixOS-Toolkit](../development/toolkit); the Toolkit is not a unified prerequisite for system operation. |
| **Watch Face Development** | [Watch Face Development Tutorial](./watchface_development) | Watch face root page, Watch Face type EPKG, installation, and switching. The Toolkit does not currently provide a watch face project template; the tutorial explains the steps to manually prepare the entry file. |
| **Platform / BSP / Vendor Integration** | [Platform and Board Integration](../integration/overview) | Core's device and port contracts, target BSP, board-level firmware, boot, and hardware integration. Choose a specific Board first, then use that project's own toolchain and build process. |
| **Core Development** | [System Architecture](../architecture/arch) and [Core Development Contract](../architecture/core_development_contract) | Core's dependency boundaries are described on the architecture page; the source code is in the [main repository](https://github.com/ElenixOS/ElenixOS/tree/main/src), and the testing and contribution process is described in the [Testing Guide](../development/testing/overview) and [Contributing Guide](../contributing). When you need a runnable target, use the [Simulator path](../simulator/overview) or the corresponding [Platform / Board project](../integration/overview). |
| **Simulator Rapid Iteration** | [Simulator Guide](../simulator/overview) | Environment, build, and run for Native / WASM desktop targets. It is an optional development auxiliary environment, not the default deployment target or board-level firmware builder. |
| **Understand the System First** | [System Architecture](../architecture/arch) | The main relationships among Core, Platform, Application, Runtime, Service, and Device. |

## Three Different Build Artifacts

- **Board-level firmware** is built and flashed by Platform / BSP projects for a specific SoC and Board. The project, toolchain, configuration, and download method are defined by the specific platform project; choose a target from the [Board-level Firmware Build Path](./build).
- **Application / Watch Face installation packages** are generated as `.epk` by the development workflow, then installed onto a system already running ElenixOS; they are not firmware images.
- **The Simulator** is built by the host toolchain as a desktop program or WASM page for auxiliary development; it does not generate Board firmware.

The public entry point ends here. The complete commands, code, configuration, deployment, and expected results for each role are located in the corresponding task tutorials; for interface queries, see the [JavaScript API Reference](../architecture/script_engine/elenix_os).

# Platform and Board Integration

ElenixOS Core provides portable Framework, Runtime, Service, Device, and port contracts; board-level projects implement these contracts and combine the SoC / BSP, peripheral drivers, boot flow, configuration, and toolchain to produce board-level firmware. Different integration projects have independent build, configuration, and flashing flows, and do not share a single set of common commands.

## Choosing an Existing Board-Level Project

| Integration Project | Target Hardware | Development and Build Entry Point |
|---|---|---|
| [ElenixOS-PSoC-E84](https://github.com/ElenixOS/ElenixOS-PSoC-E84) (in development) | PSoC Edge E84 Evaluation / AI / HMI kits; the project includes CM33 Secure, CM33 Non-secure, and CM55 multi-core projects. | Use ModusToolbox with the corresponding BSP / Toolchain; the repository README and `ElenixOS-PSoC-E84.code-workspace` describe the current project's Build, Program, and board settings. This port is not yet stable. |

The E84 integration is still in the development stage and has not yet achieved a stable port. The target board, SDK / Toolchain versions, display configuration, Linker Script, build variants, Flash layout, and flashing tools are governed by the corresponding board-level project; see [E84 Development Project Build and Flash](./psoc_edge_e84_build) for the current commands. Projects for other targets are defined by their respective Platform / Board projects. For build target selection, see [Board-Level Firmware Build Path](../getting_started/build); for porting responsibilities and registration order, see [Platform / Vendor Contract](../architecture/platform_contract); for the device interface model, see [Device Architecture](../architecture/device_architecture_design).

## Building Your Own Platform / Board Port

Existing integration projects are not the only target option. Developers can create new Platform / BSP projects for their own SoC or custom board to connect ElenixOS Core to the target hardware; there is no requirement to copy the build system or board structure of existing projects.

A porting project is responsible for implementing the applicable port and Device contracts, combining the BSP and peripherals, preparing system boot and service registration, and defining its own configuration, Toolchain, firmware artifacts, and flashing flow. For implementation boundaries, see [Platform / Vendor Contract](../architecture/platform_contract); for the overall system relationships, see [System Architecture](../architecture/arch).

## Boundary Between Firmware and Application Packages

Firmware images are built by the board-level project and flashed to the chip; an Application / Watch Face `.epk` is a Package installed on an already-running system and is not a board-level firmware artifact. For application-side project and deployment tasks, see [Application Development](../getting_started/application_development) and [Watch Face Development](../getting_started/watchface_development). The Platform integration boundary is still defined by Core's Device and port contracts and does not change based on package type.

## Optional Desktop Auxiliary Environment

[ElenixOS-Simulator](../simulator/overview) can be used to quickly validate the UI, Applications / Watch Faces, and some platform-independent logic. Native / WASM targets are built by a separate Simulator project; simulated display, input, device, and filesystem behavior cannot replace driver, power, timing, and flashing validation on the target Board.

# Watch Face Development Tutorial

This tutorial manually creates a script watch face that displays "My Watch Face", builds a Watch Face type EPKG installation package, and installs and switches watch faces on a running ElenixOS. A watch face package is not device firmware.

## Prerequisites

- Visual Studio Code 1.136 or later is installed on the host.
- [ElenixOS-Toolkit](../development/toolkit)is installed, used to build and analyze EPKG. The current Toolkit's **Create** workspace does not have a Watch Face template, so this tutorial manually creates the project files.
- There is a built and running target system: Native Simulator, or a board that provides ESH, YMODEM reception, and EPKG Installer. For the Simulator's host dependencies and build steps, see [Environment Preparation](./environment)and [Simulator Build and Run](../simulator/build); board-level firmware is handled by the target Platform / Board project.

The following commands use`$HOME`and bash/zsh. Windows users can execute directory commands in an MSYS2/MinGW shell and create files with an editor.

## 1. Create Project Files

Create the project directory and package output directory in the host terminal:```bash
mkdir -p "$HOME/ElenixOS-Watchfaces/my-clock" "$HOME/ElenixOS-Watchfaces/build"
```In VS Code, select **File > Open Folder...**, open`$HOME/ElenixOS-Watchfaces/my-clock/`, create a new root-level`manifest.json`, and write:```json
{
  "id": "com.example.clock",
  "name": "Example Clock",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "author": "Example",
  "description": "Example watch face",
  "minApiLevel": 0,
  "targetApiLevel": 0
}
````id`is the stable watch face identity used during installation and at runtime. EPKG v1 requires the manifest's identity, author, version, and API level fields; for specific semantics, see [Installation Package Format](../architecture/package_format).

Create a new root-level`main.js`in the same directory:```js
const view = eos.view.active();
const label = new lv.label(view);
label.align(lv.ALIGN_CENTER, 0, 0);
label.setText("My Watch Face");
````main.js`is the script watch face entry point;`eos.view.active()`returns the View of the current watch face root page. For the watch face root Activity, program lifecycle, and available components, see [Watch Face System](../architecture/framework/watchface).

## 2. Build and Validate the Watch Face Package

In the VS Code command palette, run **ElenixOS: Open App Tools**, open the **Build** workspace and select **Select App project**, then select`$HOME/ElenixOS-Watchfaces/my-clock/`. For Package type, select **Watch face**, and click **Validate project**; after validation passes, select **Build package**, and the output is saved as`$HOME/ElenixOS-Watchfaces/build/my-clock.epk`.

If you have added the`etk`CLI to the host`PATH`, you can run the following in any host terminal:```bash
etk package build "$HOME/ElenixOS-Watchfaces/my-clock" \
  --output "$HOME/ElenixOS-Watchfaces/build/my-clock.epk" \
  --type watchface --compression auto
etk validate "$HOME/ElenixOS-Watchfaces/build/my-clock.epk"
```A complete validation should identify the package type`watchface`, ID`com.example.clock`, and display`Validation: full`. For CLI parameters and how to obtain the tools, see [ElenixOS-Toolkit](../development/toolkit).

## 3. Install and Switch Watch Faces

Choose the path that matches the running target. The target firmware must support ESH's YMODEM reception, full EPKG validation, and Watch Face installation.

### Running on Native Simulator

First generate the Native program according to [Simulator Build and Run](../simulator/build). The following commands are executed from the`ElenixOS-Simulator`repository root:```bash
mkdir -p fs/tmp
cp "$HOME/ElenixOS-Watchfaces/build/my-clock.epk" fs/tmp/my-clock.epk
./bin/main
```Execute the following one by one at the ESH prompt in the same terminal:```text
pkg validate /tmp/my-clock.epk
pkg install /tmp/my-clock.epk
```Validation should return`pkg: valid EPKG v1`. After installation is complete, select **Example Clock** from the Watch Face list provided by the target system. In Native Simulator, you can long-press the crown control to open the list; the main page should display **My Watch Face**.

### Installing on a Running Board

In the VS Code command palette, run **ElenixOS: Open ESH Terminal** and select the device UART. The Toolkit's default serial format is 8N1, with RTS/CTS flow control disabled, and`elenixosToolkit.uartBaudRate`defaults to`921600`; the host rate must match the device side, and this configuration item can be modified in VS Code Settings.

Run **ElenixOS: Send File or Folder with YMODEM (UART)**, select`$HOME/ElenixOS-Watchfaces/build/my-clock.epk`, and set the device-side target path to`/tmp/my-clock.epk`. After the transfer is complete, execute the following in the ESH Terminal:```text
pkg validate /tmp/my-clock.epk
pkg install /tmp/my-clock.epk
```After full validation succeeds and installation is complete, long-press the current watch face to enter the Watch Face list and select **Example Clock**. If the target board does not have this long-press entry configured, use the watch face selection entry it provides; serial deployment and selection entries are determined by the Platform / Board integration.

## Next Steps

- Package contract shared by Application and Watch Face: [EPKG v1 Installation Package Format](../architecture/package_format).
- Script interface reference: [JavaScript API Reference](../architecture/script_engine/elenix_os).

# Introduction to ElenixOS

ElenixOS is an open-source embedded operating system for smartwatches and other resource-constrained wearable devices. The system Core provides the application model, runtime, Framework, system services, and device abstraction; Platform / BSP projects connect the Core to specific SoCs, Boards, displays, input, storage, and other peripherals.

ElenixOS-Simulator and ElenixOS-Toolkit are auxiliary development tools in the ecosystem: the Simulator helps rapidly iterate on UI, Application / Watch Face, and some platform-independent logic; the Toolkit initializes application projects and builds and analyzes EPKG installation packages. The Simulator's desktop runtime behavior does not represent the drivers and hardware capabilities of a specific Board.

The PSoC Edge E84 port is still in development and has not yet reached a stable port. Developers can also create their own Platform / BSP projects and port to their own SoC or Board.

## System Model

- **Application / Package:** Script applications and watch faces are delivered as EPKG installation packages, and after installation are managed by the Framework under a stable identity.
- **Program / Runtime:** SPM manages script Programs, Realms, and runtime resources; JavaScript enters the Native system through interfaces exposed by SNI.
- **Activity / View:** The Activity Controller manages page relationships and lifecycle; an Activity holds its own LVGL View. Pages and script Programs are two related but independent lifecycles.
- **Framework / Service:** The Framework provides application-facing models, and Services manage system-shared capabilities, state, and policies; Storage, Sensor, Audio, and the like are specific system services.
- **Device / Platform:** The Core defines device and platform contracts; Board / BSP integration implements these boundaries and connects to the target hardware.

For detailed relationships, see [System Architecture](./architecture/arch). The system entry page does not presume the reader's development role, nor does it require everyone to first create an Application project.

## Continue Reading

- **Choose a development target:** [Quick Start](./getting_started/quick_start) lists the Application, Watch Face, Platform / BSP, Core, Simulator, and system-understanding paths.
- **Understand system boundaries:** Read [System Architecture](./architecture/arch), then proceed as needed into Application, Platform, Core, or specific subsystem contracts.

# Simulator Build and Run

This page only covers the desktop target of ElenixOS-Simulator. The Simulator builds ElenixOS Core on the host and runs it natively or via WASM; it is not a firmware build for a specific Board. When first obtaining the code, initialize the submodules:```bash
git clone --recursive https://github.com/ElenixOS/ElenixOS-Simulator.git
cd ElenixOS-Simulator
```For an existing workspace, run:```bash
git submodule update --init --recursive
```For Native dependencies, see [Simulator Environment Preparation](../getting_started/environment). To build board-level firmware, select the target Board from [Board-Level Firmware Build Paths](../getting_started/build).

## Native

The Native build requires the SDL2 development library. Build and run with Debug:```bash
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug
cmake --build build --parallel
./bin/main
```If`build/`is already configured, you can also use the root Makefile:```bash
make
make run
```The Native simulated screen is 390×450 pixels, and the window provides crown and side button input controls; resizing the window does not change the system's logical display size.

## WASM

The WASM build requires an activated Emscripten toolchain:```bash
emcmake cmake -S . -B build-wasm -DEOS_PLATFORM=WASM -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build-wasm --parallel
```The artifacts are located in`build-wasm/bin/`, including`main.html`,`main.js`,`main.wasm`, and preloaded data files. Access via an HTTP server:```bash
cd build-wasm/bin
python3 -m http.server 8000
```Then open [http://localhost:8000/main.html](http://localhost:8000/main.html); you cannot open it directly with`file://`.

## Build Options

| Option | Default | Purpose |
|---|---:|---|
|`EOS_PLATFORM`|`Native`| Select`Native`or`WASM`|
|`USE_FREERTOS`|`OFF`| Enable FreeRTOS under Native; disabled under WASM |
|`LV_USE_DRAW_SDL`|`OFF`| Enable the SDL drawing backend, requires the corresponding SDL2_image dependency |
|`LV_USE_LIBPNG`/`LV_USE_LIBJPEG_TURBO`|`OFF`| Enable PNG / JPEG decoding support |
|`LV_USE_FFMPEG`/`LV_USE_FREETYPE`|`OFF`| Enable FFmpeg / FreeType support |
|`ASAN`|`OFF`| Enable Address / Leak / Undefined sanitizer for Debug builds |

Optional backends can only be enabled when the dependency libraries can be found by CMake.

## Kconfig

Configurations such as memory policy, fonts, display parameters, logging, and Recent Apps are managed through Kconfig:```bash
cmake -B build
cmake --build build --target menuconfig
```The configuration is saved in the current build directory`.config`, and the generated header file is located in`build/generated/`. When`menuconfig`is saved,`generated/eos_config_gen.h`in that directory is refreshed at the same time; if you edit`.config`directly, first run`cmake -B build`to regenerate the configuration header file. For the complete priority and configuration values, see [Kernel Configuration System](../development/kconfig).

## Logging and Troubleshooting

Native currently writes logs to the Simulator repository`tmp/latest.log`, and old logs are archived by time. If SDL2 cannot be found during the configuration phase, install the SDL2 development package first; if submodules are missing or linking errors occur, confirm that recursive submodule update has been executed, then reconfigure using a new build directory.

# PSoC Edge E84 Development Project Build and Flashing

This tutorial targets the current [ElenixOS-PSoC-E84 project](https://github.com/ElenixOS/ElenixOS-PSoC-E84) and the `APP_KIT_PSE84_AI` default target. This integration is still under development and has not yet formed a stable port; a successful command only indicates that the current project completed the corresponding build or download step.

## Prerequisites

- ModusToolbox is installed, along with the BSP, Middleware, and GNU Arm Toolchain used by this project.
- You have a development board and KitProg3 matching `TARGET`. Prepare board jumpers, display devices, and connection methods according to the target project instructions.
- The build environment can locate the ModusToolbox tools. The default installation path is detected by the project build files; if installed in a custom location, you need to set `CY_TOOLS_PATHS` to point to the corresponding `tools_<version>` directory.
- `CY_GETLIBS_SHARED_PATH` points to the parent directory of the shared dependency directory. The example below uses `$HOME/ModusToolbox`, and dependencies will be placed under `mtb_shared/`.

## Obtaining the Project and Building

In the host's bash/zsh shell, run the following from the parent directory where the source code is stored: ```bash
git clone --recursive https://github.com/ElenixOS/ElenixOS-PSoC-E84.git
cd ElenixOS-PSoC-E84
mkdir -p "$HOME/ModusToolbox"
make getlibs CY_GETLIBS_SHARED_PATH="$HOME/ModusToolbox"
CY_SECONDSTAGE=1 make build -j2 TARGET=APP_KIT_PSE84_AI TOOLCHAIN=GCC_ARM CONFIG=Debug \
  CY_GETLIBS_SHARED_PATH="$HOME/ModusToolbox"
``` The command is run from the root directory of the `ElenixOS-PSoC-E84` repository. Currently, `common.mk` defaults to selecting `APP_KIT_PSE84_AI`, `GCC_ARM`, and `Debug`; the command above explicitly writes out these values to make it easier to confirm the build target. The project's top-level Makefile combines the CM33 Secure, CM33 Non-secure, and CM55 projects, and a successful build should generate `build/app_combined.hex`.

When changing the Evaluation Kit, toolchain, or display module, first confirm the target values and hardware requirements in the project `common.mk`, the corresponding Board configuration, and the README. You cannot simply replace the board name in the command.

## Flashing and Booting

After confirming that the KitProg3 and development board matching the target configuration are connected, run the following in the repository root directory: ```bash
CY_SECONDSTAGE=1 make program \
  TARGET=APP_KIT_PSE84_AI TOOLCHAIN=GCC_ARM CONFIG=Debug \
  CY_GETLIBS_SHARED_PATH="$HOME/ModusToolbox"
``` This project invokes the ModusToolbox download configuration to write to the target board. Success is determined by the downloader and the target project output; then set the boot state, external display, and cables according to the board instructions. You can also open `ElenixOS-PSoC-E84.code-workspace` in VS Code and run **Terminal > Run Task > Build** and **Program Application (KitProg3)**.

The board-level project's `TARGET`, BSP, Linker Script, firmware layout, and downloader together determine the actual supported scope. The build or flashing result of this development project does not mean that E84 has become a stable port; firmware download and EPKG installation are different processes. For application-side entry points, see [Application Development](../getting_started/application_development) and [Watch Face Development](../getting_started/watchface_development).
